Chapter 7 — Optimization: Gradient Descent and Stochastic Gradient Descent

Chapter 6 ended with a loss that has no closed-form minimizer and was handled with Newton’s method, a method that needs the Hessian and a linear solve at every step. This chapter studies the cheap alternative that powers almost all of modern machine learning: follow the negative gradient. We shall see exactly how fast it converges, why the answer is governed by the same singular values that governed ridge regression, what changes when the gradient is estimated from a few examples, and why stopping early is itself a form of regularization.

7.1 Learning objectives¶

Every model of the book so far has been defined as the minimizer of a loss. Chapters 1 and 6 could find that minimizer by solving linear equations, or, for the logistic loss, with a few Newton steps. In the chapters that follow (support vector machines, boosting, neural networks) the minimizer has to be computed iteratively, with methods that use only the gradient of the loss, because the Hessian is too large to form, or because the loss is a sum over millions of examples. This chapter develops the theory and the practice of these methods on the models that we already understand, where the true minimizer is known and every claim can be checked.

After working through it you will be able to:

  1. derive the gradient of the least-squares, logistic and softmax losses, verify it by finite differences, and prove that the negative gradient is the direction of steepest descent;

  2. define smoothness (LLL), strong convexity (μ\muμ) and the condition number κ=L/μ\kappa = L/\muκ=L/μ, and compute them for the models of Chapter 6;

  3. state and prove the descent lemma, and from it the convergence of gradient descent: exact formulas on quadratics (with the step-size limit 2/L2/L2/L), the O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) rate for convex smooth functions, and the linear rate (1−μ/L)k(1 - \mu/L)^k(1−μ/L)k for strongly convex ones;

  4. explain why feature scaling speeds up the optimization (preconditioning), why Newton’s method is the ideal preconditioner, and choose a step size automatically with backtracking line search;

  5. derive momentum (heavy ball) and Nesterov acceleration, and prove that on quadratics they replace κ\kappaκ by κ\sqrt\kappaκ​;

  6. explain stochastic gradient descent: the unbiased mini-batch gradient, the noise floor of a constant step size, the O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) rate of a decreasing step size, and the cost accounting in epochs;

  7. use SGD in practice: choose the learning rate on a logarithmic grid, and recognize early stopping as an implicit form of ridge regularization and gradient descent on separable data as a path to the maximum-margin classifier;

  8. describe adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam) and what they fix and do not fix, understand the role of saddle points in non-convex problems, and choose an optimizer for a given problem.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 to 6. In particular the normal equations (Section 1.6), the eigendecomposition and the effect of feature scales (Sections 2.3.7 and 2.7.1), the conditioning of least squares (Section 6.2.3), the singular-value view of ridge (Section 6.3.2), and the logistic loss, Newton’s method and separable data (Sections 6.4.2 to 6.4.4).

A word about the data in this chapter

The experiments use real data sets, all shipped with scikit-learn: Diabetes (least squares), Breast Cancer (logistic regression), Digits (softmax regression) and two classes of Iris (a separable problem). Since the theory of this chapter is about optimization, the target of each experiment is the exact minimum of the loss, which we compute once with Newton’s method or with L-BFGS and call f∗f^\astf∗; the plots then show the suboptimality f(wk)−f∗f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\astf(wk​)−f∗, which can be measured exactly. Only two constructions are not data: the small quadratic functions used to draw the geometry of gradient descent (Section 7.3.2), and two classical test functions of non-convex optimization (Section 7.9). Both are flagged where they appear.

7.2 The problem, the gradient and the geometry¶

7.2.1 What we minimize, and the direction of steepest descent¶

In this chapter every model is a vector of parameters w∈Rp\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^pw∈Rp (the intercept included: we write w\mathbf{w}w for all the parameters, where Chapter 6 distinguished bbb and w\mathbf{w}w) and every training problem has the form

min⁡w∈Rpf(w),f(w)=1n∑i=1nℓi(w)+λ2∥w∥2,\min_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^p} f(\mathbf{w}), \qquad f(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\mathbf{w}) + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2,w∈Rpmin​f(w),f(w)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓi​(w)+2λ​∥w∥2,
(1)

the average of a loss ℓi\ell_iℓi​ per training example plus a ridge penalty. The three losses of Chapter 6 give three objectives, and each gradient has the same shape, features times residual:

Modelℓi(w)\ell_i(\mathbf{w})ℓi​(w)∇f(w)\nabla f(\mathbf{w})∇f(w) (no penalty)
Least squares12(xi⊤w−yi)2\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{w} - y_i)^221​(xi⊤​w−yi​)21nX⊤(Xw−y)\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y})n1​X⊤(Xw−y)
Logistic regressionlog⁡(1+exi⊤w)−yi xi⊤w\log(1 + e^{\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{w}}) - y_i\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{w}log(1+exi⊤​w)−yi​xi⊤​w1nX⊤(p−y)\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})n1​X⊤(p−y),  pi=σ(xi⊤w)\ p_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{w}) pi​=σ(xi⊤​w)
Softmax regression−log⁡pi,yi-\log p_{i,y_i}−logpi,yi​​1n(P−Y)⊤X\frac1n(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})^\top\mathbf{X}n1​(P−Y)⊤X

(Least squares with the factor 12\frac1221​ is the loss of Chapter 6 divided by nnn; the logistic and softmax gradients are Proposition 6.9 and Exercise 6.5; the penalty adds λw\lambda\mathbf{w}λw to each gradient.) The residual Xw−y\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}Xw−y, or p−y\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}p−y, says how wrong the model is on each example, and the gradient weighs the features by this error.

Why is the negative gradient the direction to move? Because, among all the directions of the same length, it is the one along which the function decreases fastest.

Proposition 7.1 (steepest descent)

Let fff be differentiable at w\mathbf{w}w with ∇f(w)≠0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}) \neq \mathbf{0}∇f(w)=0. For every unit vector u\mathbf{u}u, the directional derivative satisfies

−∥∇f(w)∥≤∇f(w)⊤u≤∥∇f(w)∥,-\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVert \le \nabla f(\mathbf{w})^\top\mathbf{u} \le \lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVert,−∥∇f(w)∥≤∇f(w)⊤u≤∥∇f(w)∥,
(2)

and the lower bound is attained only by u=−∇f(w)/∥∇f(w)∥\mathbf{u} = -\nabla f(\mathbf{w})/\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVertu=−∇f(w)/∥∇f(w)∥.

Proof

This is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, ∣g⊤u∣≤∥g∥ ∥u∥\lvert\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{u}\rvert \le \lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert∣g⊤u∣≤∥g∥∥u∥, with equality if and only if u\mathbf{u}u is a multiple of g\mathbf{g}g. For u=−g/∥g∥\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{g}/\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVertu=−g/∥g∥ the directional derivative equals −∥g∥-\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert−∥g∥. □\square□

The statement is about an infinitesimal step. How far to go along −∇f-\nabla f−∇f is the whole subject of this chapter. Gradient descent (GD) chooses a number η>0\eta > 0η>0, the step size or learning rate, and iterates

wk+1=wk−η ∇f(wk).\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\,\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k).wk+1​=wk​−η∇f(wk​).
(3)

Before using a gradient, verify it. The central finite difference (f(w+hej)−f(w−hej))/(2h)\big(f(\mathbf{w} + h\mathbf{e}_j) - f(\mathbf{w} - h\mathbf{e}_j)\big)/(2h)(f(w+hej​)−f(w−hej​))/(2h) approximates the jjj-th component with an error of order h2h^2h2; it costs two evaluations of fff per coordinate, so it is a testing tool and not an algorithm. The next cell loads the Diabetes data with the split used in Chapter 6 (331 training patients, standardized with the training statistics, centered target), checks the least-squares gradient and the claim of Proposition 7.1 on 100,000 random directions.

diab = load_diabetes(scaled=False)
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(diab.data, diab.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED)
scaler_d = StandardScaler().fit(Xd_tr)
Zd, Zd_te = scaler_d.transform(Xd_tr), scaler_d.transform(Xd_te)
n_d = len(yd_tr)
yd_mean = yd_tr.mean()
yd_c = yd_tr - yd_mean                       # centered target: no intercept needed
print(f"Diabetes: {n_d} training patients, {Zd.shape[1]} features")


def ls_objective(w, A, yc, lam):
    """Ridge least squares f(w) = (1/2n)||A w - yc||^2 + (lam/2)||w||^2 and its gradient."""
    r = A @ w - yc
    return 0.5 * np.mean(r**2) + 0.5 * lam * w @ w, A.T @ r / len(yc) + lam * w


def central_difference(f, w, h=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(w)
    for j in range(len(w)):
        e = np.zeros_like(w)
        e[j] = h
        g[j] = (f(w + e) - f(w - e)) / (2 * h)
    return g


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
w_try = rng.normal(size=Zd.shape[1])
f_try, g_try = ls_objective(w_try, Zd, yd_c, lam=0.1)
g_fd = central_difference(lambda w: ls_objective(w, Zd, yd_c, 0.1)[0], w_try)
print(f"relative error of the analytic gradient: {np.linalg.norm(g_try - g_fd) / np.linalg.norm(g_try):.1e}")

# Proposition 7.1: no unit direction beats -g/||g||
U = rng.normal(size=(100_000, len(w_try)))
U /= np.linalg.norm(U, axis=1, keepdims=True)
print(f"smallest directional derivative among 100,000 random unit directions: {(U @ g_try).min():.2f}")
print(f"-||g||, the value for the steepest direction                        : {-np.linalg.norm(g_try):.2f}")

7.2.2 Smoothness, strong convexity and the condition number¶

How large a step can we afford? That depends on how fast the gradient itself changes, that is on the curvature. Two numbers describe it.

Definition. A differentiable function fff is LLL-smooth if its gradient is LLL-Lipschitz: ∥∇f(x)−∇f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{y})\rVert \le L\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\rVert∥∇f(x)−∇f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥ for all x,y\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}x,y. It is μ\muμ-strongly convex if f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x)+μ2∥y−x∥2f(\mathbf{y}) \ge f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) + \frac\mu2\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}\rVert^2f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x)+2μ​∥y−x∥2 for all x,y\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}x,y (the function lies above its tangent plane by at least a parabola). The ratio

κ=Lμ≥1\kappa = \frac{L}{\mu} \ge 1κ=μL​≥1
(4)

is the condition number.

For a twice differentiable function both properties are statements about the eigenvalues of the Hessian: fff is LLL-smooth and μ\muμ-strongly convex if and only if

μI⪯∇2f(w)⪯LIfor all w.\mu\mathbf{I} \preceq \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{w}) \preceq L\mathbf{I}\qquad\text{for all } \mathbf{w}.μI⪯∇2f(w)⪯LIfor all w.
(5)

(One direction in a line: ∇f(x)−∇f(y)=Hˉ(x−y)\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{y}) = \bar{\mathbf{H}}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})∇f(x)−∇f(y)=Hˉ(x−y) with Hˉ=∫01∇2f(y+t(x−y)) dt\bar{\mathbf{H}} = \int_0^1\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{y} + t(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}))\,dtHˉ=∫01​∇2f(y+t(x−y))dt, a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues lie in [μ,L][\mu, L][μ,L], so ∥∇f(x)−∇f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{y})\rVert \le L\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\rVert∥∇f(x)−∇f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥.) For the least-squares objective of Chapter 6 the Hessian does not depend on w\mathbf{w}w:

∇2f=H=1nX⊤X+λI,L=σmax⁡2n+λ,μ=σmin⁡2n+λ,\nabla^2 f = \mathbf{H} = \frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}, \qquad L = \frac{\sigma_{\max}^2}{n} + \lambda,\quad \mu = \frac{\sigma_{\min}^2}{n} + \lambda,∇2f=H=n1​X⊤X+λI,L=nσmax2​​+λ,μ=nσmin2​​+λ,
(6)

where σmax⁡\sigma_{\max}σmax​ and σmin⁡\sigma_{\min}σmin​ are the extreme singular values of X\mathbf{X}X (Section 6.3.2). The same singular values that decided how much ridge shrinks each direction decide how curved the loss is in each direction, and a ridge penalty adds λ\lambdaλ to all the curvatures, which lowers the condition number. The next cell computes LLL, μ\muμ and κ\kappaκ for the Diabetes problem in three situations.

def hessian_spectrum(A, lam):
    """Eigenvalues (descending) of H = A^T A / n + lam I, with the columns of A centered."""
    Ac = A - A.mean(axis=0)
    return np.linalg.eigvalsh(Ac.T @ Ac / len(A) + lam * np.eye(A.shape[1]))[::-1]


cases = {
    "raw units, lambda = 0": hessian_spectrum(Xd_tr, 0.0),
    "standardized, lambda = 0": hessian_spectrum(Zd, 0.0),
    "standardized, lambda = 0.1": hessian_spectrum(Zd, 0.1),
    "standardized, lambda = 1": hessian_spectrum(Zd, 1.0),
}
cond_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {name: {"L": ev[0], "mu": ev[-1], "kappa": ev[0] / ev[-1]} for name, ev in cases.items()}
).T
print(cond_table.to_string(formatters={"L": "{:.4g}".format, "mu": "{:.4g}".format, "kappa": "{:.4g}".format}))
                               L       mu     kappa
raw units, lambda = 0       2092  0.02814 7.434e+04
standardized, lambda = 0   3.919 0.009379     417.8
standardized, lambda = 0.1 4.019   0.1094     36.74
standardized, lambda = 1   4.919    1.009     4.873

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
    ranks = np.arange(1, 11)
    styles = [("raw units, lambda = 0", VERMILION, "o", "raw units, $\\lambda = 0$"),

    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()

figure_7_1()

The conditioning of the raw problem is κ≈7⋅104\kappa \approx 7 \cdot 10^4κ≈7⋅104: the curvature in the steepest direction is 2092 and in the flattest only 0.028. Almost all of it is an accident of units (the columns of the raw data are measured in years, kilograms, milligrams per decilitre, and so on); standardizing the features brings κ\kappaκ down to 418 without changing the model at all, and the remaining ill-conditioning is the collinearity of the blood-serum variables that Section 6.2.3 diagnosed. A ridge penalty of λ=0.1\lambda = 0.1λ=0.1 lowers it to 37 and λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 to 4.9. We shall see in the next sections that κ\kappaκ is, up to constants, the number of gradient steps that a first-order method needs per factor of eee of accuracy.

For the logistic loss the Hessian 1nX⊤SX+λI\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}n1​X⊤SX+λI depends on w\mathbf{w}w through the weights si=pi(1−pi)∈(0,14]s_i = p_i(1 - p_i) \in (0, \tfrac14]si​=pi​(1−pi​)∈(0,41​] (Section 6.4.2). Since si≤14s_i \le \tfrac14si​≤41​, the loss is LLL-smooth globally with L=σmax⁡2/(4n)+λL = \sigma_{\max}^2/(4n) + \lambdaL=σmax2​/(4n)+λ, a bound that we shall find to be very pessimistic near the solution (Section 7.3.4). Strong convexity holds only with the constant μ=λ\mu = \lambdaμ=λ plus a term that decays to zero as the probabilities approach 0 and 1; for this reason the ridge penalty matters for the optimization as much as for the statistics.

7.3 Gradient descent¶

7.3.1 The descent lemma¶

The workhorse of every convergence proof in this chapter is the following inequality. It says that an LLL-smooth function lies below a parabola built on its tangent plane, which is exactly what we need to know that a small step cannot overshoot too much.

Proposition 7.2 (descent lemma)

If fff is LLL-smooth, then for all x,y\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}x,y,

f(y)≤f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x)+L2∥y−x∥2.f(\mathbf{y}) \le f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) + \frac L2\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}\rVert^2 .f(y)≤f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x)+2L​∥y−x∥2.
(7)

Consequently a gradient step x+=x−η∇f(x)\mathbf{x}^+ = \mathbf{x} - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{x})x+=x−η∇f(x) satisfies

f(x+)≤f(x)−η(1−Lη2)∥∇f(x)∥2,f(\mathbf{x}^+) \le f(\mathbf{x}) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{L\eta}{2}\Big)\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\rVert^2 ,f(x+)≤f(x)−η(1−2Lη​)∥∇f(x)∥2,
(8)

so the function decreases whenever 0<η<2/L0 < \eta < 2/L0<η<2/L, and for η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L it decreases by at least η2∥∇f(x)∥2\frac\eta2\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\rVert^22η​∥∇f(x)∥2.

Proof

By the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from x\mathbf{x}x to y\mathbf{y}y,

f(y)−f(x)−∇f(x)⊤(y−x)=∫01(∇f(x+t(y−x))−∇f(x))⊤(y−x) dt.f(\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) = \int_0^1\big(\nabla f(\mathbf{x} + t(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x})) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x})\big)^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x})\,dt .f(y)−f(x)−∇f(x)⊤(y−x)=∫01​(∇f(x+t(y−x))−∇f(x))⊤(y−x)dt.
(9)

By Cauchy–Schwarz and the Lipschitz property, the integrand is at most Lt∥y−x∥2Lt\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}\rVert^2Lt∥y−x∥2, and ∫01Lt dt=L/2\int_0^1 Lt\,dt = L/2∫01​Ltdt=L/2. For the gradient step put y=x−η∇f(x)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{x})y=x−η∇f(x): the linear term is −η∥∇f∥2-\eta\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2−η∥∇f∥2 and the quadratic term is Lη22∥∇f∥2\frac{L\eta^2}{2}\lVert\nabla f\rVert^22Lη2​∥∇f∥2. If η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L then 1−Lη/2≥121 - L\eta/2 \ge \frac121−Lη/2≥21​. □\square□

The lemma already explains the limit that we shall meet in every experiment: the guarantee of decrease disappears at η=2/L\eta = 2/Lη=2/L.

7.3.2 Gradient descent on a quadratic¶

The quadratic f(w)=12w⊤Hw−b⊤wf(\mathbf{w}) = \frac12\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{w}f(w)=21​w⊤Hw−b⊤w with H≻0\mathbf{H} \succ 0H≻0 is both the least-squares objective and the second-order Taylor model of any smooth loss near its minimum, so it is the right place to understand GD exactly. Its gradient is Hw−b\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{b}Hw−b and its minimizer is w∗=H−1b\mathbf{w}^\ast = \mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{b}w∗=H−1b.

Theorem 7.3 (gradient descent on a quadratic)

Let H=VΛV⊤\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{V}^\topH=VΛV⊤ have eigenvalues μ=λp≤⋯≤λ1=L\mu = \lambda_p \le \dots \le \lambda_1 = Lμ=λp​≤⋯≤λ1​=L (all positive) and let cj=vj⊤(w0−w∗)c_j = \mathbf{v}_j^\top(\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast)cj​=vj⊤​(w0​−w∗). Gradient descent with step size η\etaη produces

For 0<η<2/L0 < \eta < 2/L0<η<2/L, ∥wk−w∗∥≤ρ(η)k∥w0−w∗∥\lVert\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert \le \rho(\eta)^k\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert∥wk​−w∗∥≤ρ(η)k∥w0​−w∗∥ with ρ(η)=max⁡{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣}\rho(\eta) = \max\{\lvert 1 - \eta\mu\rvert, \lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert\}ρ(η)=max{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣}, and this is the best possible constant.

Proof

The gradient is H(w−w∗)\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}^\ast)H(w−w∗), so with ek=wk−w∗\mathbf{e}_k = \mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\astek​=wk​−w∗ the iteration is ek+1=(I−ηH)ek\mathbf{e}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{I} - \eta\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}_kek+1​=(I−ηH)ek​. In the eigenbasis of H\mathbf{H}H each coordinate evolves on its own, vj⊤ek+1=(1−ηλj)vj⊤ek\mathbf{v}_j^\top\mathbf{e}_{k+1} = (1 - \eta\lambda_j)\mathbf{v}_j^\top\mathbf{e}_kvj⊤​ek+1​=(1−ηλj​)vj⊤​ek​, which gives the formula; the value formula follows from f(w)−f(w∗)=12e⊤Hef(\mathbf{w}) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) = \frac12\mathbf{e}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{e}f(w)−f(w∗)=21​e⊤He.

All the coordinates converge if and only if η<2/λ1=2/L\eta < 2/\lambda_1 = 2/Lη<2/λ1​=2/L. If η>2/L\eta > 2/Lη>2/L then ∣1−ηL∣>1\lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert > 1∣1−ηL∣>1 and the first coordinate grows geometrically.

(3) The function η↦max⁡{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣}\eta \mapsto \max\{\lvert 1 - \eta\mu\rvert, \lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert\}η↦max{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣} decreases while 1−ημ1 - \eta\mu1−ημ dominates and increases afterwards; the minimum is where 1−ημ=ηL−11 - \eta\mu = \eta L - 11−ημ=ηL−1, that is η=2/(L+μ)\eta = 2/(L + \mu)η=2/(L+μ), and then ρ=1−2μ/(L+μ)=(L−μ)/(L+μ)\rho = 1 - 2\mu/(L + \mu) = (L - \mu)/(L + \mu)ρ=1−2μ/(L+μ)=(L−μ)/(L+μ).

For ρ=1−1/κ\rho = 1 - 1/\kappaρ=1−1/κ, ln⁡(1/ρ)≥1/κ\ln(1/\rho) \ge 1/\kappaln(1/ρ)≥1/κ. For ρ=(κ−1)/(κ+1)\rho = (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)ρ=(κ−1)/(κ+1), ln⁡(1/ρ)=2 artanh(1/κ)≥2/κ\ln(1/\rho) = 2\,\mathrm{artanh}(1/\kappa) \ge 2/\kappaln(1/ρ)=2artanh(1/κ)≥2/κ. □\square□

Three consequences are worth keeping in mind. First, the step size has a hard ceiling that depends only on the largest curvature, 2/L2/L2/L; the smallest curvature, on the contrary, decides how long the iteration takes. Second, GD is a filter: after kkk steps the component of the error along the jjj-th eigenvector has been multiplied by (1−ηλj)k(1 - \eta\lambda_j)^k(1−ηλj​)k, so the directions of high curvature converge first and the flat directions last. Section 7.7.2 turns this observation into a statement about regularization. Third, the best achievable rate (κ−1)/(κ+1)(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)(κ−1)/(κ+1) is close to 1 when κ\kappaκ is large: no choice of step size can rescue an ill-conditioned problem, which is the motivation for Sections 7.4 and 7.5.

Worked example 7.1 — gradient descent on f(w)=12(w12+10 w22)f(\mathbf{w}) = \frac12(w_1^2 + 10\,w_2^2)f(w)=21​(w12​+10w22​)¶

(This is a constructed function, chosen to make the arithmetic exact.) Here H=diag(1,10)\mathbf{H} = \mathrm{diag}(1, 10)H=diag(1,10), so μ=1\mu = 1μ=1, L=10L = 10L=10, κ=10\kappa = 10κ=10, w∗=0\mathbf{w}^\ast = \mathbf{0}w∗=0, and we start from w0=(10,1.5)\mathbf{w}_0 = (10, 1.5)w0​=(10,1.5). By Theorem 7.3 the coordinates evolve independently, w1,k=(1−η)k⋅10w_{1,k} = (1 - \eta)^k\cdot 10w1,k​=(1−η)k⋅10 and w2,k=(1−10η)k⋅1.5w_{2,k} = (1 - 10\eta)^k\cdot 1.5w2,k​=(1−10η)k⋅1.5.

  • Step size η=1/L=0.1\eta = 1/L = 0.1η=1/L=0.1. The second factor is 1−10⋅0.1=01 - 10\cdot 0.1 = 01−10⋅0.1=0: the steep coordinate is annihilated in a single step, and the iteration then creeps along the flat coordinate with factor 0.9. To reduce the error by 10-6 we need k≥ln⁡106/ln⁡(1/0.9)=13.82/0.1054=131.1k \ge \ln 10^6/\ln(1/0.9) = 13.82/0.1054 = 131.1k≥ln106/ln(1/0.9)=13.82/0.1054=131.1, that is 132 iterations.

  • Best step size η∗=2/11=0.1818\eta^\ast = 2/11 = 0.1818η∗=2/11=0.1818. The factors are 9/11=0.8189/11 = 0.8189/11=0.818 and −9/11-9/11−9/11: both coordinates shrink at the same rate, the second one changing sign at every step (zigzag). The rate is ρ=(κ−1)/(κ+1)=9/11\rho = (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1) = 9/11ρ=(κ−1)/(κ+1)=9/11 and k≥13.82/ln⁡(11/9)=13.82/0.2007=68.9k \ge 13.82/\ln(11/9) = 13.82/0.2007 = 68.9k≥13.82/ln(11/9)=13.82/0.2007=68.9, that is 69 iterations, half as many.

  • Step size η=0.05\eta = 0.05η=0.05 (small and safe): factors 0.95 and 0.5; the rate is 0.95 and 270 iterations are needed. A step that is too small wastes iterations.

  • Step size η=0.19=1.9/L\eta = 0.19 = 1.9/Lη=0.19=1.9/L (just below the ceiling 0.2): factors 0.81 and -0.9; the steep coordinate oscillates and decays slowly, ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9; the bound predicts 131 iterations and the iteration needs 114 (the oscillating coordinate starts at 1.5 and not at 10, so the bound is not attained). Beyond η=0.2\eta = 0.2η=0.2 the second coordinate is multiplied by a number smaller than -1 at every step and the iteration diverges.

H_toy = np.diag([1.0, 10.0])
w0_toy = np.array([10.0, 1.5])
L_toy, mu_toy = 10.0, 1.0
rows = []
for eta in [0.05, 0.1, 2 / 11, 0.19, 0.21]:
    rho = max(abs(1 - eta * mu_toy), abs(1 - eta * L_toy))
    w = w0_toy.copy()
    k_hit = None
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        for k in range(1, 2001):
            w = w - eta * (H_toy @ w)
            if np.linalg.norm(w) < 1e-6 * np.linalg.norm(w0_toy):
                k_hit = k
                break
    pred = np.log(1e6) / np.log(1 / rho) if rho < 1 else np.inf
    rows.append({"eta": eta, "rho": rho, "predicted k": pred, "measured k": k_hit if k_hit else "diverges"})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))

def figure_7_2():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.4, 3.6), sharey=True)
    g1, g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-11, 11, 300), np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 300))
    F = 0.5 * (g1**2 + 10 * g2**2)
    for ax, eta, title in zip(axes, [0.05, 2 / 11, 0.19],
                              [r"$\eta = 0.05$: too small", r"$\eta = 2/(L+\mu)$: best", r"$\eta = 0.19$: near the ceiling $2/L$"]):
        path = [w0_toy]
        for _ in range(25):
            path.append(path[-1] - eta * (H_toy @ path[-1]))
        path = np.array(path)

        ax.plot(0, 0, "*", color=VERMILION, ms=12, mec="white")

Now the same measurements on a real problem. The least-squares objective of the standardized Diabetes data with λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 has L=3.92L = 3.92L=3.92, μ=0.0094\mu = 0.0094μ=0.0094 and κ=418\kappa = 418κ=418 (Section 7.2.2). We run gradient descent from w0=0\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}w0​=0 with four step sizes: the “safe” 1/L1/L1/L, the optimal 2/(L+μ)2/(L + \mu)2/(L+μ), a step just below the ceiling, 1.9/L1.9/L1.9/L, and one just above, 2.1/L2.1/L2.1/L. For each we compare the number of iterations needed to reduce the distance to w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ by a factor 10-6 with the prediction ln⁡(106)/ln⁡(1/ρ)\ln(10^6)/\ln(1/\rho)ln(106)/ln(1/ρ) of Theorem 7.3.

H_d = Zd.T @ Zd / n_d                      # lambda = 0
b_d = Zd.T @ yd_c / n_d
w_star_d = np.linalg.solve(H_d, b_d)
ev_d = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H_d)
L_d, mu_d = ev_d[-1], ev_d[0]
kappa_d = L_d / mu_d
print(f"L = {L_d:.4f}, mu = {mu_d:.5f}, kappa = {kappa_d:.1f}, kappa*ln(10^6) = {kappa_d * np.log(1e6):.0f}")


def gd_quadratic(H, b, w0, eta, iters, w_star):
    """Distance ||w_k - w*|| for k = 0..iters (gradient descent on 1/2 w'Hw - b'w)."""
    w, errs = w0.copy(), np.empty(iters + 1)
    errs[0] = np.linalg.norm(w - w_star)
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        for k in range(iters):
            w = w - eta * (H @ w - b)
            errs[k + 1] = np.linalg.norm(w - w_star)
    return errs


rules = {"1/L": 1 / L_d, "2/(L+mu)": 2 / (L_d + mu_d), "1.9/L": 1.9 / L_d, "2.1/L": 2.1 / L_d}
err_curves, rows = {}, []
for name, eta in rules.items():
    errs = gd_quadratic(H_d, b_d, np.zeros(len(b_d)), eta, 20_000, w_star_d)
    err_curves[name] = errs
    rho = max(abs(1 - eta * mu_d), abs(1 - eta * L_d))
    hit = np.flatnonzero(errs < 1e-6 * errs[0])
    rows.append({"step size": name, "eta": eta, "rho": rho,
                 "predicted iterations": np.log(1e6) / np.log(1 / rho) if rho < 1 else np.inf,
                 "measured iterations": int(hit[0]) if len(hit) else "diverges"})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.5g}"))

# Figure 7.3 — measured error and the bound rho^k, Diabetes least squares (lambda = 0)
def figure_7_3():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
    ks = np.arange(20_001)
    for (name, color, label) in [("1/L", BLUE, r"$\eta = 1/L$"), ("2/(L+mu)", GREEN, r"$\eta = 2/(L+\mu)$"),
                                 ("1.9/L", ORANGE, r"$\eta = 1.9/L$")]:
        eta = rules[name]
        rho = max(abs(1 - eta * mu_d), abs(1 - eta * L_d))
        rel = err_curves[name] / err_curves[name][0]
        ax.plot(ks, rel, color=color, lw=2, label=label)
        ax.plot(ks, rho**ks, color=color, lw=1.2, ls="--")
    ax.axhline(1e-6, color="0.4", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set(yscale="log", xlim=(0, 6500), ylim=(1e-8, 3),
           xlabel="iteration $k$", ylabel=r"$\|\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\| / \|\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\|$",
           title="Solid: measured. Dashed: the bound $\\rho^k$ of Theorem 7.3")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_3()

7.3.3 Convergence for convex and strongly convex functions¶

Real losses are not quadratic, but the descent lemma lets us prove two guarantees that hold for every convex LLL-smooth function. The first needs nothing beyond convexity and gives a sublinear rate; the second adds strong convexity and gives a linear (geometric) rate, in the same form as for quadratics.

Theorem 7.4 (gradient descent, convex case)

Let fff be convex and LLL-smooth with a minimizer w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗, and let 0<η≤1/L0 < \eta \le 1/L0<η≤1/L. Then gradient descent satisfies, for every k≥1k \ge 1k≥1,

f(wk)−f(w∗)≤∥w0−w∗∥22ηk.f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) \le \frac{\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2}{2\eta k}.f(wk​)−f(w∗)≤2ηk∥w0​−w∗∥2​.
(11)
Proof

Write gk=∇f(wk)\mathbf{g}_k = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)gk​=∇f(wk​). By the descent lemma (Proposition 7.2), f(wk+1)≤f(wk)−η2∥gk∥2f(\mathbf{w}_{k+1}) \le f(\mathbf{w}_k) - \frac\eta2\lVert\mathbf{g}_k\rVert^2f(wk+1​)≤f(wk​)−2η​∥gk​∥2, and by convexity f(wk)≤f(w∗)+gk⊤(wk−w∗)f(\mathbf{w}_k) \le f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) + \mathbf{g}_k^\top(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast)f(wk​)≤f(w∗)+gk⊤​(wk​−w∗). Combining,

f(wk+1)−f(w∗)≤gk⊤(wk−w∗)−η2∥gk∥2=12η(∥wk−w∗∥2−∥wk−ηgk−w∗∥2),f(\mathbf{w}_{k+1}) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) \le \mathbf{g}_k^\top(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast) - \frac\eta2\lVert\mathbf{g}_k\rVert^2 = \frac1{2\eta}\Big(\lVert\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf{w}_k - \eta\mathbf{g}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2\Big),f(wk+1​)−f(w∗)≤gk⊤​(wk​−w∗)−2η​∥gk​∥2=2η1​(∥wk​−w∗∥2−∥wk​−ηgk​−w∗∥2),
(12)

where the identity is obtained by expanding ∥a−ηg∥2=∥a∥2−2η g⊤a+η2∥g∥2\lVert\mathbf{a} - \eta\mathbf{g}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert^2 - 2\eta\,\mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{a} + \eta^2\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert^2∥a−ηg∥2=∥a∥2−2ηg⊤a+η2∥g∥2 with a=wk−w∗\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\asta=wk​−w∗. The last norm is ∥wk+1−w∗∥2\lVert\mathbf{w}_{k+1} - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2∥wk+1​−w∗∥2. Summing over k=0,…,K−1k = 0, \dots, K - 1k=0,…,K−1 the right-hand side telescopes:

∑k=1K(f(wk)−f(w∗))≤∥w0−w∗∥2−∥wK−w∗∥22η≤∥w0−w∗∥22η.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\big(f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast)\big) \le \frac{\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf{w}_K - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2}{2\eta} \le \frac{\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2}{2\eta}.k=1∑K​(f(wk​)−f(w∗))≤2η∥w0​−w∗∥2−∥wK​−w∗∥2​≤2η∥w0​−w∗∥2​.
(13)

Since f(wk)f(\mathbf{w}_k)f(wk​) is non-increasing, the last term of the sum is the smallest, and K (f(wK)−f(w∗))K\,(f(\mathbf{w}_K) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast))K(f(wK​)−f(w∗)) is at most the sum. □\square□

The rate O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) means that halving the suboptimality costs a doubling of the number of iterations: to reach an accuracy ε\varepsilonε we need O(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon)O(1/ε) steps. Strong convexity improves this to O(log⁡1/ε)O(\log 1/\varepsilon)O(log1/ε).

Theorem 7.5 (gradient descent, strongly convex case)

Let fff be twice continuously differentiable with μI⪯∇2f⪯LI\mu\mathbf{I} \preceq \nabla^2 f \preceq L\mathbf{I}μI⪯∇2f⪯LI everywhere, and let w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ be its minimizer. For 0<η<2/L0 < \eta < 2/L0<η<2/L, gradient descent satisfies

∥wk−w∗∥≤ρk∥w0−w∗∥,ρ=max⁡{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣},\lVert\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert \le \rho^k\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert, \qquad \rho = \max\{\lvert 1 - \eta\mu\rvert, \lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert\},∥wk​−w∗∥≤ρk∥w0​−w∗∥,ρ=max{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣},
(14)

that is ρ=1−ημ\rho = 1 - \eta\muρ=1−ημ for η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L and ρ=κ−1κ+1\rho = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}ρ=κ+1κ−1​ for η=2L+μ\eta = \frac2{L + \mu}η=L+μ2​: exactly the rates of Theorem 7.3 for quadratics.

Proof

Since ∇f(w∗)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) = \mathbf{0}∇f(w∗)=0, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives ∇f(wk)=Hˉk(wk−w∗)\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k) = \bar{\mathbf{H}}_k(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast)∇f(wk​)=Hˉk​(wk​−w∗) with Hˉk=∫01∇2f(w∗+t(wk−w∗)) dt\bar{\mathbf{H}}_k = \int_0^1\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{w}^\ast + t(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast))\,dtHˉk​=∫01​∇2f(w∗+t(wk​−w∗))dt, a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues in [μ,L][\mu, L][μ,L]. Therefore wk+1−w∗=(I−ηHˉk)(wk−w∗)\mathbf{w}_{k+1} - \mathbf{w}^\ast = (\mathbf{I} - \eta\bar{\mathbf{H}}_k)(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast)wk+1​−w∗=(I−ηHˉk​)(wk​−w∗), and the eigenvalues of I−ηHˉk\mathbf{I} - \eta\bar{\mathbf{H}}_kI−ηHˉk​ lie in [1−ηL,1−ημ][1 - \eta L, 1 - \eta\mu][1−ηL,1−ημ], so its spectral norm is at most ρ\rhoρ. Induction on kkk completes the proof. □\square□

Two remarks. The linear rate needs the curvature bounds to hold along the whole path; for the logistic loss they hold locally near the solution, with constants that are very different from the global ones, as the experiment below shows. And both theorems are guarantees, that is upper bounds valid for every function of the class: a particular problem may converge much faster.

Worked example 7.2 — a one-parameter logistic problem¶

Take the two training points x=−1x = -1x=−1 with y=0y = 0y=0 and x=1x = 1x=1 with y=1y = 1y=1, no intercept, and minimize the mean logistic loss f(w)=log⁡(1+e−w)f(w) = \log(1 + e^{-w})f(w)=log(1+e−w) (the problem of Exercise 6.3(b), divided by 2). The derivatives are f′(w)=−σ(−w)f'(w) = -\sigma(-w)f′(w)=−σ(−w) and f′′(w)=σ(w)σ(−w)≤14f''(w) = \sigma(w)\sigma(-w) \le \tfrac14f′′(w)=σ(w)σ(−w)≤41​, so the function is LLL-smooth with L=14L = \tfrac14L=41​ and the “safe” step is η=1/L=4\eta = 1/L = 4η=1/L=4. The data are separable, so fff has no minimizer (f→0f \to 0f→0 as w→∞w \to \inftyw→∞).

Gradient step from w0=0w_0 = 0w0​=0. f′(0)=−12f'(0) = -\tfrac12f′(0)=−21​, so w1=0+4⋅12=2w_1 = 0 + 4\cdot\tfrac12 = 2w1​=0+4⋅21​=2, and f(w1)=log⁡(1+e−2)=0.127f(w_1) = \log(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.127f(w1​)=log(1+e−2)=0.127 against f(w0)=log⁡2=0.693f(w_0) = \log 2 = 0.693f(w0​)=log2=0.693. The descent lemma guarantees a decrease of at least η/2⋅f′(0)2=2⋅14=12\eta/2\cdot f'(0)^2 = 2\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac12η/2⋅f′(0)2=2⋅41​=21​, so f(w1)≤0.193f(w_1) \le 0.193f(w1​)≤0.193: true, with room to spare.

Newton step from w0=0w_0 = 0w0​=0. f′′(0)=14f''(0) = \tfrac14f′′(0)=41​ coincides with LLL, so the Newton step −f′/f′′-f'/f''−f′/f′′ is also +2. The two methods agree at the first step and then part ways: at w1=2w_1 = 2w1​=2, f′(2)=−0.119f'(2) = -0.119f′(2)=−0.119 and f′′(2)=0.105f''(2) = 0.105f′′(2)=0.105, so GD moves by 4⋅0.119=0.484\cdot 0.119 = 0.484⋅0.119=0.48 and Newton by 0.119/0.105=1.130.119/0.105 = 1.130.119/0.105=1.13. The next cell shows the first iterations: Newton adds about 1 at every step (the recursion wt+1=wt+1+e−wtw_{t+1} = w_t + 1 + e^{-w_t}wt+1​=wt​+1+e−wt​ of Exercise 6.3), while GD slows down because the gradient decays like e−we^{-w}e−w and wkw_kwk​ grows like log⁡k\log klogk. We shall meet this slow logarithmic growth again, on real data, in Section 7.7.3.

def f_toy(w):
    return np.log1p(np.exp(-w))

7.3.4 An experiment: gradient descent on a logistic regression¶

We now measure everything on a real problem: the regularized logistic regression of Section 6.5 on the Breast Cancer data (malignant =1= 1=1; the stratified training set of 426 patients of Chapter 6; the 30 features standardized; an unpenalized intercept), with λ=0.01\lambda = 0.01λ=0.01, that is C=1/(λn)=0.23C = 1/(\lambda n) = 0.23C=1/(λn)=0.23. We first compute the exact minimum f∗f^\astf∗ with Newton’s method (Section 6.4.3), so that every later run can report its suboptimality f(wk)−f∗f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\astf(wk​)−f∗, and we compute the two kinds of curvature constants: the global bound of Section 7.2.2 and the actual curvature at the minimizer.

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
Xb = bc.data.to_numpy()
yb = (1 - bc.target).to_numpy().astype(float)           # malignant = 1, as in Chapter 6
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=yb)
scaler_b = StandardScaler().fit(Xb_tr)
Zb = scaler_b.transform(Xb_tr)
n_b, d_b = Zb.shape
Zb1 = np.c_[np.ones(n_b), Zb]                           # a column of ones for the intercept
pen_b = np.r_[0.0, np.ones(d_b)]                        # the intercept is not penalized
lam_b = 0.01
print(f"Breast Cancer: {n_b} training patients, {d_b} features, lambda = {lam_b} (C = {1 / (lam_b * n_b):.2f})")


def logistic_obj(w, idx=None, lam=lam_b):
    """Mean logistic loss + (lam/2)||w||^2 (intercept excluded) and its gradient, on all or on a subset of rows."""
    A, y = (Zb1, yb_tr) if idx is None else (Zb1[idx], yb_tr[idx])
    s = A @ w
    f = np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, s) - y * s) + 0.5 * lam * np.sum(pen_b * w**2)
    return f, A.T @ (expit(s) - y) / len(y) + lam * pen_b * w


def logistic_hessian(w, lam=lam_b):
    p = expit(Zb1 @ w)
    return (Zb1.T * (p * (1 - p))) @ Zb1 / n_b + lam * np.diag(pen_b)


g_chk = np.random.default_rng(SEED).normal(size=d_b + 1)
g_fd = central_difference(lambda w: logistic_obj(w)[0], g_chk)
print(f"relative error of the analytic gradient: {np.linalg.norm(logistic_obj(g_chk)[1] - g_fd) / np.linalg.norm(g_fd):.1e}")

# the exact minimizer, by Newton's method
w_star_b = np.zeros(d_b + 1)
for _ in range(30):
    w_star_b = w_star_b - np.linalg.solve(logistic_hessian(w_star_b), logistic_obj(w_star_b)[1])
f_star_b = logistic_obj(w_star_b)[0]
print(f"f* = {f_star_b:.8f}, norm of the gradient at w*: {np.linalg.norm(logistic_obj(w_star_b)[1]):.1e}")

L_glob = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Zb1.T @ Zb1 / n_b)[-1] / 4 + lam_b     # global bound, valid everywhere
ev_loc = np.linalg.eigvalsh(logistic_hessian(w_star_b))
L_loc, mu_loc = ev_loc[-1], ev_loc[0]
print(f"global smoothness bound  L_glob = {L_glob:.4f}   (2/L_glob = {2 / L_glob:.3f})")
print(f"curvature at the minimizer: L_loc = {L_loc:.4f}, mu_loc = {mu_loc:.4f}, kappa_loc = {L_loc / mu_loc:.1f}   (2/L_loc = {2 / L_loc:.2f})")
Breast Cancer: 426 training patients, 30 features, lambda = 0.01 (C = 0.23)
relative error of the analytic gradient: 4.5e-10
f* = 0.10212875, norm of the gradient at w*: 1.4e-17
global smoothness bound  L_glob = 3.2955   (2/L_glob = 0.607)
curvature at the minimizer: L_loc = 0.2294, mu_loc = 0.0097, kappa_loc = 23.7   (2/L_loc = 8.72)

The global bound is L=3.30L = 3.30L=3.30, but at the minimizer the largest curvature is 0.23, fourteen times smaller: the bound is correct (it must hold at the worst point, which is the origin, where every sis_isi​ equals 14\frac1441​) and nevertheless very pessimistic near the solution, because there most training points are classified with confidence and pi(1−pi)p_i(1 - p_i)pi​(1−pi​) is tiny. The theory therefore predicts that steps up to 2/Lglob=0.612/L_{\text{glob}} = 0.612/Lglob​=0.61 are safe, and the local theory (Theorem 7.3 applied to the Taylor model at w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗) predicts that the iteration is stable up to 2/Lloc=8.72/L_{\text{loc}} = 8.72/Lloc​=8.7. We test both claims.

def iterations_to(gaps, tol=1e-8):
    """First iteration after which the suboptimality stays below tol, or 'not reached'."""
    above = np.flatnonzero(gaps >= tol)
    k = int(above[-1]) + 1 if len(above) else 0
    return k if k < len(gaps) else "not reached"


def gd_logistic(eta, iters=3000, w0=None):
    """Gradient descent on the logistic objective; returns the suboptimality f(w_k) - f* for k = 0..iters-1."""
    w = np.zeros(d_b + 1) if w0 is None else w0.copy()
    gaps = np.empty(iters)
    for k in range(iters):
        f, g = logistic_obj(w)
        gaps[k] = f - f_star_b
        if not np.isfinite(f) or gaps[k] > 1e6:
            gaps[k:] = np.inf
            break
        w = w - eta * g
    return gaps


etas = {"1/L_glob = 0.30": 1 / L_glob, "1": 1.0, "3": 3.0, "8": 8.0, "8.7": 8.7, "9": 9.0, "10": 10.0}
gd_runs, rows = {}, []
for name, eta in etas.items():
    gaps = gd_logistic(eta)
    gd_runs[name] = gaps
    rows.append({"eta": name, "iterations to gap < 1e-8": iterations_to(gaps),
                 "final gap": gaps[-1], "largest gap": gaps[np.isfinite(gaps)].max()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
            eta iterations to gap < 1e-8  final gap  largest gap
1/L_glob = 0.30                     1631   1.04e-12        0.591
              1                      497  -1.39e-17        0.591
              3                      171          0        0.591
              8                       69          0         1.22
            8.7                       65          0         1.39
              9              not reached    0.00352         1.47
             10              not reached   0.000241         1.74

The step 1/Lglob=0.301/L_{\text{glob}} = 0.301/Lglob​=0.30 that the global theory recommends works, and needs 1,631 iterations; the step η=8\eta = 8η=8, twenty-six times larger and far beyond the global ceiling 0.61, needs only 69, because the iteration is governed by the local conditioning. The threshold is where the local theory puts it: η=8.7<2/Lloc=8.72\eta = 8.7 < 2/L_{\text{loc}} = 8.72η=8.7<2/Lloc​=8.72 still converges (in 65 iterations, the fastest of the convergent runs), while η=9\eta = 9η=9 and η=10\eta = 10η=10 do not. Note how η=9\eta = 9η=9 fails: the iterates come within 10-8 of the minimum at iteration 63, but the minimum is now an unstable fixed point (the error is multiplied by 1−9 Lloc=−1.061 - 9\,L_{\text{loc}} = -1.061−9Lloc​=−1.06 per step in the steepest direction), so they are pushed away again and end in a cycle (final gap 3.5⋅10−33.5 \cdot 10^{-3}3.5⋅10−3). The loss does not explode, because the logistic function grows only linearly. The practical lesson is that the safe step of the theory is conservative by a large factor, and that the right step size is something to be found, which is what line search (Section 7.3.5) and the learning-rate grid of Section 7.7.1 do.

# Figure 7.4 — gradient descent on the logistic loss: the step size decides everything
def figure_7_4():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
    for name, color, ls in [("1/L_glob = 0.30", BLUE, "-"), ("1", SKY, "-"), ("8", GREEN, "-"), ("9", VERMILION, "-")]:
        gaps = gd_runs[name]
        ax.plot(np.arange(len(gaps)), gaps, color=color, lw=2, ls=ls,
                label=(r"$\eta = 1/L_{\mathrm{glob}} = 0.30$" if name.startswith("1/") else rf"$\eta = {name}$"))
    ax.axhline(1e-8, color="0.4", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set(yscale="log", xlim=(0, 1800), ylim=(1e-10, 3),
           xlabel="iteration $k$", ylabel=r"suboptimality $f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast$",
           title="Breast Cancer, logistic regression, $\\lambda = 0.01$")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_4()

How do the theorems of Section 7.3.3 compare with the measurement? For η=1/Lglob\eta = 1/L_{\text{glob}}η=1/Lglob​, Theorem 7.4 guarantees f(wk)−f∗≤∥w0−w∗∥2/(2ηk)f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast \le \lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2/(2\eta k)f(wk​)−f∗≤∥w0​−w∗∥2/(2ηk), valid because the loss is convex and LglobL_{\text{glob}}Lglob​-smooth. Theorem 7.5 does not apply globally (the unpenalized intercept direction has no uniform lower curvature), but near w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ the function behaves like the quadratic with curvatures [μloc,Lloc][\mu_{\text{loc}}, L_{\text{loc}}][μloc​,Lloc​], so the suboptimality of the final phase should decay like (1−ημloc)2k(1 - \eta\mu_{\text{loc}})^{2k}(1−ημloc​)2k, the square of the rate of the distance.

eta_g = 1 / L_glob
gaps = gd_logistic(eta_g, 3000)
ks = np.arange(1, len(gaps))
dist0 = np.linalg.norm(w_star_b)                         # ||w_0 - w*|| with w_0 = 0
bound_74 = dist0**2 / (2 * eta_g * ks)

late = np.log(gaps[1200] / gaps[1000]) / 200
print(f"measured asymptotic decay per iteration of the gap, k = 1000..1200: {np.exp(late):.5f}")

# Figure 7.5 — a guarantee versus a measurement
def figure_7_5():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
    ax.plot(ks, gaps[1:], color=BLUE, lw=2, label="measured, $\\eta = 1/L_{\\mathrm{glob}}$")
    ax.plot(ks, bound_74, color=VERMILION, lw=2, ls="--", label=r"Theorem 7.4: $\|\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\|^2/(2\eta k)$")
    ref = gaps[1000] * rate_loc ** (2 * (ks - 1000))
    ax.plot(ks[900:], ref[900:], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=":", label=r"local rate $(1 - \eta\mu_{\mathrm{loc}})^{2k}$, anchored at $k = 1000$")
    ax.set(yscale="log", xscale="log", xlim=(1, 3000), ylim=(1e-10, 1e3),
           xlabel="iteration $k$", ylabel=r"suboptimality $f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast$",

figure_7_5()

The bound holds at every iteration, as it must, and it is loose by many orders of magnitude after a few hundred iterations: the measured curve bends downward into a straight line on the log scale, the signature of linear convergence, at the rate predicted by the local curvature. A guarantee tells us what cannot go wrong; it does not predict the speed on a given problem.

7.3.5 Choosing the step size automatically: backtracking line search¶

Both theorems say “take η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L”, and we have just seen that the LLL of the theory can be an order of magnitude too large. Backtracking line search finds a good step at run time with the descent lemma as its only tool. Fix constants c∈(0,1)c \in (0, 1)c∈(0,1) (typically 10-4) and β∈(0,1)\beta \in (0, 1)β∈(0,1) (typically 12\tfrac1221​); at each iteration start from a trial step η0\eta_0η0​ and multiply it by β\betaβ until the Armijo condition

f(w−ηg)≤f(w)−c η ∥g∥2,g=∇f(w),f(\mathbf{w} - \eta\mathbf{g}) \le f(\mathbf{w}) - c\,\eta\,\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert^2, \qquad \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}),f(w−ηg)≤f(w)−cη∥g∥2,g=∇f(w),
(15)

holds (the decrease must be at least a fraction ccc of what the tangent promises).

Proposition 7.6 (backtracking terminates)

If fff is LLL-smooth and g≠0\mathbf{g} \ne \mathbf{0}g=0, the Armijo condition holds for every step η≤2(1−c)/L\eta \le 2(1 - c)/Lη≤2(1−c)/L. Consequently backtracking stops after finitely many reductions, and the accepted step satisfies η≥min⁡{η0, 2β(1−c)/L}\eta \ge \min\{\eta_0,\ 2\beta(1 - c)/L\}η≥min{η0​, 2β(1−c)/L}.

Proof

By Proposition 7.2, f(w−ηg)≤f(w)−η(1−Lη/2)∥g∥2f(\mathbf{w} - \eta\mathbf{g}) \le f(\mathbf{w}) - \eta(1 - L\eta/2)\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert^2f(w−ηg)≤f(w)−η(1−Lη/2)∥g∥2, and 1−Lη/2≥c1 - L\eta/2 \ge c1−Lη/2≥c if and only if η≤2(1−c)/L\eta \le 2(1 - c)/Lη≤2(1−c)/L. If η0\eta_0η0​ is already below this threshold it is accepted. Otherwise the loop stops at the first η0βj\eta_0\beta^jη0​βj below the threshold, and the previous trial, η0βj−1\eta_0\beta^{j-1}η0​βj−1, was above it, so the accepted value exceeds β⋅2(1−c)/L\beta\cdot 2(1 - c)/Lβ⋅2(1−c)/L. □\square□

So backtracking never takes a step smaller than a fixed fraction of 1/L1/L1/L, and the proofs of Theorems 7.4 and 7.5 go through with that step: the guarantees of the best constant step are kept without knowing LLL. A practical refinement, used below, is to warm-start the search by doubling the last accepted step: the step then tracks the local curvature, increasing when the function is flat and shrinking when it is not. Each trial costs one evaluation of the function (but not of the gradient).

For comparison we also run two methods that use curvature information. L-BFGS (limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno, available as scipy.optimize.minimize(method="L-BFGS-B")) builds an approximation of the inverse Hessian from the last few gradient differences, at the cost of a few vectors, and is the default solver of LogisticRegression. Newton’s method (Section 6.4.3) computes the exact Hessian and solves a linear system at every step.

def gd_backtracking(tol=1e-8, eta0=1.0, c=1e-4, beta=0.5, max_iter=3000):
    """GD with Armijo backtracking, warm-started by doubling the last accepted step."""
    w = np.zeros(d_b + 1)
    eta, gaps, n_func, etas = eta0, [], 0, []
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        f, g = logistic_obj(w)
        n_func += 1
        gaps.append(f - f_star_b)
        etas.append(eta)
        if gaps[-1] < tol:
            break
        eta *= 2
        while True:
            f_new = logistic_obj(w - eta * g)[0]
            n_func += 1
            if f_new <= f - c * eta * (g @ g):
                break
            eta *= beta
        w = w - eta * g
    return np.array(gaps), n_func, etas


gaps_bt, n_func_bt, etas_bt = gd_backtracking()
print(f"backtracking: {len(gaps_bt) - 1} gradient steps, {n_func_bt} function evaluations, "
      f"accepted steps from {etas_bt[1]:.2f} to {etas_bt[-2]:.2f}")

# L-BFGS, counting evaluations and recording the gap after every iteration
evals_lbfgs, hist_lbfgs = [0], []
def fun_counted(w):
    evals_lbfgs[0] += 1
    return logistic_obj(w)


def record(w):
    hist_lbfgs.append((logistic_obj(w)[0] - f_star_b, evals_lbfgs[0]))


res = minimize(fun_counted, np.zeros(d_b + 1), jac=True, method="L-BFGS-B", callback=record,
               options={"maxiter": 500, "gtol": 1e-12, "ftol": 1e-16})
hist = np.array(hist_lbfgs)
k_lb = int(np.flatnonzero(hist[:, 0] < 1e-8)[0])
print(f"L-BFGS: gap below 1e-8 after {k_lb + 1} iterations and {int(hist[k_lb, 1])} gradient evaluations")

# Newton
w, newton_gaps = np.zeros(d_b + 1), []
for _ in range(8):
    f, g = logistic_obj(w)
    newton_gaps.append(f - f_star_b)
    w = w - np.linalg.solve(logistic_hessian(w), g)
newton_gaps.append(logistic_obj(w)[0] - f_star_b)
print("Newton, gap after k steps (k = 0..8):", " ".join(f"{v:.1e}" for v in newton_gaps))
backtracking: 57 gradient steps, 169 function evaluations, accepted steps from 2.00 to 8.00
L-BFGS: gap below 1e-8 after 19 iterations and 21 gradient evaluations
Newton, gap after k steps (k = 0..8): 5.9e-01 1.5e-01 6.0e-02 1.7e-02 2.1e-03 5.0e-05 3.6e-08 2.2e-14 0.0e+00

With the warm start, backtracking finds on its own steps that grow to 8, close to the best constant step (8.7, the edge of the stable range), and reaches the target in 57 steps (and 169 function evaluations, of which 111 are the extra trials: backtracking spends about three function evaluations per step to save more than a thousand steps). L-BFGS is faster still, 19 iterations (21 evaluations of the function and the gradient), because it also corrects the direction. Newton needs 7 steps and then converges quadratically: from 3.6⋅10−83.6 \cdot 10^{-8}3.6⋅10−8 to 2⋅10−142 \cdot 10^{-14}2⋅10−14 in a single step. The price is the cost of an iteration: a gradient costs of the order of n pn\,pnp operations, and a Newton step needs the Hessian (n p2n\,p^2np2) and a solve (p3p^3p3), about p=31p = 31p=31 times more here, and a great deal more for the millions of parameters of a neural network, where the Hessian cannot even be stored. Section 7.10 collects these comparisons.

7.4 Conditioning and preprocessing¶

Theorem 7.3 says that the number of iterations is proportional to κ\kappaκ, and Section 7.2.2 found that the raw Diabetes problem has κ=7⋅104\kappa = 7 \cdot 10^4κ=7⋅104 against 418 after standardization. The next result explains why rescaling the variables is the same as changing the optimization method.

Proposition 7.7 (rescaling is preconditioning)

Let fff be differentiable, D\mathbf{D}D an invertible matrix, and g(v)=f(Dv)g(\mathbf{v}) = f(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{v})g(v)=f(Dv). Gradient descent on ggg, vk+1=vk−η∇g(vk)\mathbf{v}_{k+1} = \mathbf{v}_k - \eta\nabla g(\mathbf{v}_k)vk+1​=vk​−η∇g(vk​), produces, in the original variables wk=Dvk\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{v}_kwk​=Dvk​, the iteration

wk+1=wk−η M ∇f(wk),M=DD⊤≻0,\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\,\mathbf{M}\,\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k), \qquad \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top \succ 0,wk+1​=wk​−ηM∇f(wk​),M=DD⊤≻0,
(16)

called preconditioned gradient descent. If fff is quadratic with Hessian H\mathbf{H}H, the Hessian of ggg is D⊤HD\mathbf{D}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}D⊤HD, whose eigenvalues are those of MH\mathbf{M}\mathbf{H}MH, and the speed of the iteration is governed by κ(MH)=κ(D⊤HD)\kappa(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{H}) = \kappa(\mathbf{D}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D})κ(MH)=κ(D⊤HD).

Proof

By the chain rule ∇g(v)=D⊤∇f(Dv)\nabla g(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{D}^\top\nabla f(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{v})∇g(v)=D⊤∇f(Dv), so wk+1=Dvk+1=wk−ηDD⊤∇f(wk)\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{v}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)wk+1​=Dvk+1​=wk​−ηDD⊤∇f(wk​). For a quadratic, ∇2g=D⊤HD\nabla^2 g = \mathbf{D}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}∇2g=D⊤HD. The matrices D⊤HD\mathbf{D}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}D⊤HD and DD⊤H\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top\mathbf{H}DD⊤H are similar (conjugate by D\mathbf{D}D), hence they have the same eigenvalues. □\square□

Two examples show the range of the idea. Standardization is a diagonal preconditioner. Dividing column jjj of the (centered) design matrix by its standard deviation sjs_jsj​ is a change of variables w=Dv\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{v}w=Dv with D=diag(1/sj)\mathbf{D} = \mathrm{diag}(1/s_j)D=diag(1/sj​), and since the diagonal of the Hessian 1nX⊤X\frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}n1​X⊤X is exactly sj2s_j^2sj2​, the preconditioner M=diag(1/sj2)\mathbf{M} = \mathrm{diag}(1/s_j^2)M=diag(1/sj2​) is the inverse of the diagonal of H\mathbf{H}H (the Jacobi preconditioner). Newton’s method is the perfect preconditioner. Take M=H−1\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{H}^{-1}M=H−1: then MH=I\mathbf{M}\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{I}MH=I, κ=1\kappa = 1κ=1, and with η=1\eta = 1η=1 a quadratic is solved in one step. All the second-order methods of Section 7.3.5 are attempts to approximate H−1\mathbf{H}^{-1}H−1 at a price lower than the Hessian itself.

The next cell checks Proposition 7.7 on the Diabetes data, running the iteration in the raw units with the Jacobi preconditioner and in the standardized units, and then uses the exact formula of Theorem 7.3 to count the iterations that gradient descent needs in the four situations of Section 7.2.2 (with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L for each, starting from w=0\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}w=0) to reduce the distance to the minimizer by a factor 103. Using the formula is legitimate because the objective is exactly quadratic, and it lets us count iterations in the hundreds of thousands without running them; the cell first checks the formula against a direct run of 3000 iterations.

# Proposition 7.7: gradient descent on standardized variables = preconditioned gradient descent on raw variables
Xc_raw = Xd_tr - Xd_tr.mean(axis=0)
s_raw = Xd_tr.std(axis=0)                                    # the scale used by StandardScaler
H_raw, b_raw = Xc_raw.T @ Xc_raw / n_d, Xc_raw.T @ yd_c / n_d
M_jacobi = np.diag(1 / s_raw**2)
print("diagonal of the raw Hessian equals the variances of the columns:", np.allclose(np.diag(H_raw), s_raw**2))

eta_std = 1 / L_d                                            # L_d: largest eigenvalue of the standardized Hessian
v = np.zeros(10)
w_pre = np.zeros(10)
for _ in range(200):
    v = v - eta_std * (H_d @ v - b_d)                         # standardized variables
    w_pre = w_pre - eta_std * M_jacobi @ (H_raw @ w_pre - b_raw)   # raw variables, preconditioned
print(f"largest difference between D v_200 and the preconditioned iterate: {np.abs(v / s_raw - w_pre).max():.1e}")


def quad_curves(H, b, ks, eta):
    """Exact distance ||w_k - w*|| / ||w_0 - w*|| and suboptimality of GD from w = 0 on 1/2 w'Hw - b'w, for the
    iteration counts ks, from the eigen-decomposition of Theorem 7.3."""
    ev, V = np.linalg.eigh(H)
    c = V.T @ np.linalg.solve(H, b)                           # coordinates of w_0 - w* = -w*, up to sign
    shrink = (1 - eta * ev[None, :]) ** (2 * ks[:, None])
    return np.sqrt((shrink * c[None, :] ** 2).sum(axis=1) / (c**2).sum()), 0.5 * (shrink * ev[None, :] * c[None, :] ** 2).sum(axis=1)


# check the formulas against a direct run of 3000 iterations (standardized, lambda = 0)
ks_chk = np.arange(0, 3001)
w_run, dist_run, gap_run = np.zeros(10), [], []
for _ in ks_chk:
    e = w_run - w_star_d
    dist_run.append(np.linalg.norm(e) / np.linalg.norm(w_star_d))
    gap_run.append(0.5 * e @ H_d @ e)
    w_run = w_run - (1 / L_d) * (H_d @ w_run - b_d)
dist_formula, gap_formula = quad_curves(H_d, b_d, ks_chk, 1 / L_d)
print(f"largest relative difference, distance: {np.max(np.abs(np.array(dist_run) - dist_formula) / dist_formula):.1e}, "
      f"suboptimality: {np.max(np.abs(np.array(gap_run) - gap_formula) / gap_formula):.1e}")
diagonal of the raw Hessian equals the variances of the columns: True
largest difference between D v_200 and the preconditioned iterate: 1.6e-13
largest relative difference, distance: 1.9e-12, suboptimality: 3.9e-12

setups = [("raw units, lambda = 0", H_raw, b_raw, 0.0),
          ("standardized, lambda = 0", H_d, b_d, 0.0),
          ("standardized, lambda = 0.1", H_d + 0.1 * np.eye(10), b_d, 0.1),
          ("standardized, lambda = 1", H_d + 1.0 * np.eye(10), b_d, 1.0)]
ks_log = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 7.5, 4000).astype(np.int64))
rows, gap_curves = [], {}
for name, H, b, lam in setups:
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)
    eta = 1 / ev[-1]
    dist, _ = quad_curves(H, b, ks_log, eta)
    gap_curves[name] = (ks_log, dist)
    k_hit = ks_log[np.flatnonzero(dist < 1e-3)[0]]
    rows.append({"problem": name, "kappa": ev[-1] / ev[0], "iterations": k_hit, "iterations / kappa": k_hit / (ev[-1] / ev[0])})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))

# Figure 7.6 — preconditioning by standardization, and the effect of the ridge penalty on the speed of GD
def figure_7_6():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
    for (name, (kk, gg)), color in zip(gap_curves.items(), [VERMILION, BLUE, GREEN, PURPLE]):
        label = name.replace("lambda", r"$\lambda$")
        ax.plot(kk, gg, color=color, lw=2, label=label)
    ax.axhline(1e-3, color="0.4", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlim=(1, 3e6), ylim=(1e-6, 2),
           xlabel="iteration $k$ (step size $1/L$)", ylabel=r"$\|\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\ast\| / \|\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\|$",
           title="Diabetes least squares: conditioning decides the iteration count")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

The raw problem needs 509,391509{,}391509,391 iterations to bring the iterate within a thousandth of the distance to the minimizer, the standardized problem 2,7992{,}7992,799, and the standardized problem with λ=0.1\lambda = 0.1λ=0.1 and λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 only 176 and 15. For the first two, the ratio of iterations to κ\kappaκ is 6.9=ln⁡1036.9 = \ln 10^36.9=ln103, which is the worst case κln⁡(1/ε)\kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon)κln(1/ε) of Theorem 7.3 with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L (the starting error has weight along the flattest direction); with the ridge penalty the ratio is smaller because the starting error has little weight there. Standardizing the features made gradient descent about 180 times faster without changing the model or its solution, and each additional ridge penalty makes it faster again, because adding λ\lambdaλ to every eigenvalue is precisely a reduction of κ\kappaκ (Section 7.2.2): the penalty that stabilizes the statistics in Chapter 6 also stabilizes the optimization.

Pitfall — an optimizer that “stops moving” has not necessarily converged

On the raw Diabetes features the distance to the minimizer is still essentially unchanged after 104 iterations (Figure 7.6): the iteration is crawling along a long, almost flat valley, and a stopping rule based only on the change of the loss is easily fooled by it. Two defenses: standardize the features before using any iterative solver, and monitor the norm of the gradient (which is zero at a minimizer of a smooth convex function) in addition to the change of the loss. Scikit-learn’s iterative solvers use tolerances of this kind and raise a ConvergenceWarning when max_iter is exhausted: that warning means “this is not the minimizer”, and it deserves attention.

7.5 Momentum and acceleration¶

Theorem 7.3 and Figure 7.6 deliver a sobering message: on an ill-conditioned problem the best constant step cannot beat the rate (κ−1)/(κ+1)(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)(κ−1)/(κ+1). The iteration is slow because the gradient points mostly across the narrow valley (the zigzag of Figure 7.2) and only a little along it. Momentum uses the memory of the previous steps: the components of the gradient that keep changing sign cancel, those that keep the same sign add up.

The heavy-ball method (Polyak, 1964) adds to the gradient step a fraction β∈[0,1)\beta \in [0, 1)β∈[0,1) of the previous displacement,

wk+1=wk−η∇f(wk)+β(wk−wk−1),\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k) + \beta(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}_{k-1}),wk+1​=wk​−η∇f(wk​)+β(wk​−wk−1​),
(17)

which is the discretization of a ball rolling in the landscape fff with friction (the velocity is vk+1=βvk−η∇f(wk)\mathbf{v}_{k+1} = \beta\mathbf{v}_k - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)vk+1​=βvk​−η∇f(wk​) and the position wk+1=wk+vk+1\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k + \mathbf{v}_{k+1}wk+1​=wk​+vk+1​). Nesterov’s accelerated gradient (1983) evaluates the gradient at the point reached by the momentum step instead of at the current point:

yk=wk+βk(wk−wk−1),wk+1=yk−η∇f(yk).\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{w}_k + \beta_k(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}_{k-1}), \qquad \mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{y}_k - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{y}_k).yk​=wk​+βk​(wk​−wk−1​),wk+1​=yk​−η∇f(yk​).
(18)

Both need one gradient per iteration and one extra vector of memory. For quadratics the gain is exactly the replacement of κ\kappaκ by κ\sqrt\kappaκ​.

Theorem 7.8 (heavy ball on a quadratic)

Let f(w)=12w⊤Hw−b⊤wf(\mathbf{w}) = \frac12\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{w}f(w)=21​w⊤Hw−b⊤w with the eigenvalues of H\mathbf{H}H in [μ,L][\mu, L][μ,L], and let

η=4(L+μ)2,β=(κ−1κ+1)2.\eta = \frac{4}{(\sqrt L + \sqrt\mu)^2}, \qquad \beta = \Big(\frac{\sqrt\kappa - 1}{\sqrt\kappa + 1}\Big)^2 .η=(L​+μ​)24​,β=(κ​+1κ​−1​)2.
(19)

Then every eigen-component of the error wk−w∗\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}^\astwk​−w∗ is bounded by a constant times (k+1)ρk(k + 1)\rho^k(k+1)ρk, with

ρ=β=κ−1κ+1.\rho = \sqrt\beta = \frac{\sqrt\kappa - 1}{\sqrt\kappa + 1} .ρ=β​=κ​+1κ​−1​.
(20)

To reduce the error by a factor ε\varepsilonε the method needs about κ2ln⁡(1/ε)\frac{\sqrt\kappa}{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)2κ​​ln(1/ε) iterations (up to the factor k+1k + 1k+1, which is logarithmic in the count), against κ2ln⁡(1/ε)\frac\kappa2\ln(1/\varepsilon)2κ​ln(1/ε) for the best gradient descent.

Proof

In the eigenbasis of H\mathbf{H}H the iteration decouples. For the eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ, the error component eke_kek​ satisfies ek+1=(1+β−ηλ)ek−βek−1e_{k+1} = (1 + \beta - \eta\lambda)e_k - \beta e_{k-1}ek+1​=(1+β−ηλ)ek​−βek−1​, a linear recursion of order two whose behavior is governed by the roots of z2−(1+β−ηλ)z+β=0z^2 - (1 + \beta - \eta\lambda)z + \beta = 0z2−(1+β−ηλ)z+β=0. Their product is β\betaβ. If the discriminant is negative, (1+β−ηλ)2<4β(1 + \beta - \eta\lambda)^2 < 4\beta(1+β−ηλ)2<4β, the roots are complex conjugates and both have modulus β\sqrt\betaβ​; if it is zero there is a double root of modulus β\sqrt\betaβ​ and eke_kek​ grows like (k+1)β k(k + 1)\sqrt\beta^{\,k}(k+1)β​k. The condition ∣1+β−ηλ∣≤2β\lvert 1 + \beta - \eta\lambda\rvert \le 2\sqrt\beta∣1+β−ηλ∣≤2β​ is equivalent to (1−β)2≤ηλ≤(1+β)2(1 - \sqrt\beta)^2 \le \eta\lambda \le (1 + \sqrt\beta)^2(1−β​)2≤ηλ≤(1+β​)2. With the stated β\betaβ one has β=(κ−1)/(κ+1)\sqrt\beta = (\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)β​=(κ​−1)/(κ​+1), hence (1−β)2=4/(κ+1)2=ημ(1 - \sqrt\beta)^2 = 4/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)^2 = \eta\mu(1−β​)2=4/(κ​+1)2=ημ and (1+β)2=4κ/(κ+1)2=ηL(1 + \sqrt\beta)^2 = 4\kappa/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)^2 = \eta L(1+β​)2=4κ/(κ​+1)2=ηL. Every λ∈[μ,L]\lambda \in [\mu, L]λ∈[μ,L] therefore lies in the range, and all the components contract at the rate β\sqrt\betaβ​ (up to the polynomial factor). Finally ln⁡(1/ρ)=2 artanh(1/κ)≥2/κ\ln(1/\rho) = 2\,\mathrm{artanh}(1/\sqrt\kappa) \ge 2/\sqrt\kappaln(1/ρ)=2artanh(1/κ​)≥2/κ​. □\square□

Nesterov’s method is more remarkable because its guarantee holds for every smooth convex function, not only for quadratics, and it cannot be improved by any method that uses only gradients.

Theorem 7.9 (Nesterov, 1983; stated without proof)

Let fff be convex and LLL-smooth. Accelerated gradient with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L and βk=k/(k+3)\beta_k = k/(k + 3)βk​=k/(k+3) satisfies

f(wk)−f(w∗)≤2L∥w0−w∗∥2(k+1)2,f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f(\mathbf{w}^\ast) \le \frac{2L\lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2}{(k + 1)^2} ,f(wk​)−f(w∗)≤(k+1)22L∥w0​−w∗∥2​,
(21)

an O(1/k2)O(1/k^2)O(1/k2) rate against the O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) of Theorem 7.4. If fff is also μ\muμ-strongly convex, the choice β=(κ−1)/(κ+1)\beta = (\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)β=(κ​−1)/(κ​+1) with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L gives a suboptimality of order (1−1/κ)k(1 - 1/\sqrt\kappa)^k(1−1/κ​)k, that is O(κlog⁡(1/ε))O(\sqrt\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))O(κ​log(1/ε)) iterations. These rates are optimal for first-order methods in the worst case (Nemirovski and Yudin, 1983).

(The proof, by “estimate sequences”, is in Nesterov’s book Lectures on Convex Optimization, 2018, and a short proof by a Lyapunov argument is in Bubeck’s monograph; both are listed under Further reading.) A caution: unlike gradient descent with η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L, momentum methods are not descent methods: the objective can go up for a few iterations before it goes down faster.

We check the κ\sqrt\kappaκ​ on the two problems of this chapter. First, the Diabetes least-squares problem (κ=418\kappa = 418κ=418, κ=20.4\sqrt\kappa = 20.4κ​=20.4), with the parameters of Theorems 7.3 and 7.8 and the strongly convex version of Nesterov’s method.

def momentum_run(grad, record, w0, eta, beta_fn, iters, kind):
    """Heavy ball ('hb'), Nesterov ('nag') or plain gradient descent (beta = 0); returns record(w_k), k = 0..iters-1."""
    w, w_prev, out = w0.copy(), w0.copy(), np.empty(iters)
    for k in range(iters):
        out[k] = record(w)
        if kind == "hb":
            w_new = w - eta * grad(w) + beta_fn(k) * (w - w_prev)
        else:
            y = w + beta_fn(k) * (w - w_prev)
            w_new = y - eta * grad(y)
        w_prev, w = w, w_new
    return out

eta_hb = 4 / (np.sqrt(L_d) + np.sqrt(mu_d)) ** 2
beta_hb = ((sk - 1) / (sk + 1)) ** 2
beta_nag = (sk - 1) / (sk + 1)

    "gradient descent, eta = 1/L":           (1 / L_d, lambda k: 0.0, "hb"),

    "heavy ball (Theorem 7.8)":              (eta_hb, lambda k: beta_hb, "hb"),
    "Nesterov, strongly convex version":      (1 / L_d, lambda k: beta_nag, "nag"),

7.6 Stochastic gradient descent¶

7.6.1 The stochastic gradient¶

The objective of supervised learning is an average over the training set, f(w)=1n∑iℓi(w)+λ2∥w∥2f(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell_i(\mathbf{w}) + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2f(w)=n1​∑i​ℓi​(w)+2λ​∥w∥2, and its gradient is the average of nnn per-example gradients plus the penalty gradient. Computing it costs a pass over all the data; when nnn is in the millions, or the data do not fit in memory, this is too much to pay for a single small step. The key observation of stochastic gradient descent (SGD, Robbins and Monro, 1951) is that an average can be estimated from a few terms. At each iteration draw a random mini-batch Bk\mathcal{B}_kBk​ of BBB indices and move along

gk=1B∑i∈Bk∇ℓi(wk)+λwk,wk+1=wk−ηk gk.\mathbf{g}_k = \frac1B\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_k}\nabla\ell_i(\mathbf{w}_k) + \lambda\mathbf{w}_k, \qquad \mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta_k\,\mathbf{g}_k .gk​=B1​i∈Bk​∑​∇ℓi​(wk​)+λwk​,wk+1​=wk​−ηk​gk​.
(22)

The two extreme cases have names: B=1B = 1B=1 is “pure” SGD and B=nB = nB=n is full-batch gradient descent. The next result says what the estimate is worth.

Proposition 7.10 (the mini-batch gradient)

Let the BBB indices be drawn independently and uniformly from {1,…,n}\{1, \dots, n\}{1,…,n} (with replacement) and let ui=∇ℓi(w)\mathbf{u}_i = \nabla\ell_i(\mathbf{w})ui​=∇ℓi​(w), with mean uˉ=∇f(w)−λw\bar{\mathbf{u}} = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}) - \lambda\mathbf{w}uˉ=∇f(w)−λw and per-example variance σ2(w)=1n∑i∥ui−uˉ∥2\sigma^2(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1n\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{u}_i - \bar{\mathbf{u}}\rVert^2σ2(w)=n1​∑i​∥ui​−uˉ∥2. Then

E[g]=∇f(w),E ∥g−∇f(w)∥2=σ2(w)B.\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{g}] = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}), \qquad \mathbb{E}\,\lVert\mathbf{g} - \nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVert^2 = \frac{\sigma^2(\mathbf{w})}{B}.E[g]=∇f(w),E∥g−∇f(w)∥2=Bσ2(w)​.
(23)

If the indices are drawn without replacement the variance is multiplied by (n−B)/(n−1)≤1(n - B)/(n - 1) \le 1(n−B)/(n−1)≤1, and it is zero for B=nB = nB=n.

Proof

The batch gradient is the mean of BBB independent copies of a random vector that equals ui\mathbf{u}_iui​ with probability 1/n1/n1/n; its mean is uˉ\bar{\mathbf{u}}uˉ (the penalty term is deterministic) and the variance of the mean of independent vectors is the variance of one divided by BBB. Without replacement the draws are negatively correlated, and the classical finite-population correction applies. □\square□

Two consequences. The mini-batch gradient is unbiased, so on average SGD moves like GD; and its noise decreases only like 1/B1/B1/B, that is the standard deviation like 1/B1/\sqrt B1/B​: to halve the noise one needs four times as many examples per step. Moreover the variance σ2(w)\sigma^2(\mathbf{w})σ2(w) does not vanish at the minimizer: at w∗\mathbf{w}^\astw∗ the average of the per-example gradients is (minus the penalty gradient, hence) small, but each example still pulls in its own direction. This is the origin of the noise floor of Section 7.6.2.

def example_gradients(w):
    """n x p matrix whose rows are the gradients of the individual logistic losses (without the penalty)."""
    return Zb1 * (expit(Zb1 @ w) - yb_tr)[:, None]

At the minimizer the full gradient of the data term is small (it only balances the penalty), but the per-example variance is not: the noise of SGD does not die out as we approach the solution.

7.6.2 How fast does SGD converge?¶

To measure the effect of the noise we need an assumption on it. Assume that fff is LLL-smooth and μ\muμ-strongly convex, that the stochastic gradient is unbiased, E[gk∣wk]=∇f(wk)\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{g}_k \mid \mathbf{w}_k] = \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)E[gk​∣wk​]=∇f(wk​), and that its variance is bounded, E[∥gk−∇f(wk)∥2∣wk]≤σ2\mathbb{E}[\lVert\mathbf{g}_k - \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)\rVert^2 \mid \mathbf{w}_k] \le \sigma^2E[∥gk​−∇f(wk​)∥2∣wk​]≤σ2 (for mini-batches, σ2\sigma^2σ2 stands for the per-example variance divided by BBB, by Proposition 7.10). The proofs use one more fact about strongly convex functions.

Lemma (Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality). If fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex, then ∥∇f(w)∥2≥2μ (f(w)−f∗)\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVert^2 \ge 2\mu\,(f(\mathbf{w}) - f^\ast)∥∇f(w)∥2≥2μ(f(w)−f∗) for all w\mathbf{w}w. Proof. Minimize both sides of the strong-convexity inequality f(y)≥f(w)+∇f(w)⊤(y−w)+μ2∥y−w∥2f(\mathbf{y}) \ge f(\mathbf{w}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{w})^\top(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{w}) + \frac\mu2\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{w}\rVert^2f(y)≥f(w)+∇f(w)⊤(y−w)+2μ​∥y−w∥2 over y\mathbf{y}y: the right side is minimized at y=w−∇f(w)/μ\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{w} - \nabla f(\mathbf{w})/\muy=w−∇f(w)/μ, with value f(w)−∥∇f(w)∥2/(2μ)f(\mathbf{w}) - \lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w})\rVert^2/(2\mu)f(w)−∥∇f(w)∥2/(2μ), and the left side at y=w∗\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{w}^\asty=w∗ has value f∗f^\astf∗. □\square□

Theorem 7.11 (SGD with a constant step size)

Under these assumptions, SGD with a constant step 0<η≤1/L0 < \eta \le 1/L0<η≤1/L satisfies

E[f(wk)]−f∗≤(1−ημ)k (f(w0)−f∗)+Lησ22μ.\mathbb{E}\big[f(\mathbf{w}_k)\big] - f^\ast \le (1 - \eta\mu)^k\,\big(f(\mathbf{w}_0) - f^\ast\big) + \frac{L\eta\sigma^2}{2\mu}.E[f(wk​)]−f∗≤(1−ημ)k(f(w0​)−f∗)+2μLησ2​.

Apply the descent lemma (Proposition 7.2) to the random step −ηgk-\eta\mathbf{g}_k−ηgk​, and take the expectation conditionally on wk\mathbf{w}_kwk​. E[f(wk+1)∣wk]≤f(wk)−η(1−Lη2)∥∇f(wk)∥2+Lη2σ22≤f(wk)−η2∥∇f(wk)∥2+Lη2σ22,\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{w}_{k+1}) \mid \mathbf{w}_k] \le f(\mathbf{w}_k) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{L\eta}2\Big)\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)\rVert^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}2 \le f(\mathbf{w}_k) - \frac\eta2\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)\rVert^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}2,E[f(wk+1​)∣wk​]≤f(wk​)−η(1−2Lη​)∥∇f(wk​)∥2+2Lη2σ2​≤f(wk​)−2η​∥∇f(wk​)∥2+2Lη2σ2​,

using η≤1/L\eta \le 1/Lη≤1/L. The bound has two terms. The first forgets the starting point at the same linear rate as gradient descent. The second is an error floor proportional to ησ2\eta\sigma^2ησ2: with a constant step SGD does not converge to the minimum, it hovers around it at a distance fixed by the step size and by the noise. Reducing the step lowers the floor in proportion, and lengthens the time 1/(ημ)1/(\eta\mu)1/(ημ) needed to reach it. Since σ2\sigma^2σ2 is the per-example variance divided by BBB, the floor is proportional to η/B\eta/Bη/B: when the batch is multiplied by mmm, the same floor is obtained with a step mmm times larger (the “linear scaling rule”, valid while η\etaη stays below 1/L1/L1/L).

The way out of the trade-off is to shrink the step as the iteration proceeds.

Theorem 7.12 (SGD with a decreasing step size)

Under the same assumptions, let ηk=β/(γ+k)\eta_k = \beta/(\gamma + k)ηk​=β/(γ+k) with β>1/μ\beta > 1/\muβ>1/μ and γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0 such that η0=β/γ≤1/L\eta_0 = \beta/\gamma \le 1/Lη0​=β/γ≤1/L. Then for every k≥0k \ge 0k≥0

E[f(wk)]−f∗≤νγ+k,ν=max⁡{β2Lσ22(βμ−1), γ (f(w0)−f∗)}.\mathbb{E}\big[f(\mathbf{w}_k)\big] - f^\ast \le \frac{\nu}{\gamma + k}, \qquad \nu = \max\Big\{\frac{\beta^2L\sigma^2}{2(\beta\mu - 1)},\ \gamma\,(f(\mathbf{w}_0) - f^\ast)\Big\}.E[f(wk​)]−f∗≤γ+kν​,ν=max{2(βμ−1)β2Lσ2​, γ(f(w0​)−f∗)}.
(28)
Proof

The one-step inequality of the previous proof holds with ηk\eta_kηk​ in place of η\etaη: δk+1≤(1−ηkμ)δk+Lηk2σ2/2\delta_{k+1} \le (1 - \eta_k\mu)\delta_k + L\eta_k^2\sigma^2/2δk+1​≤(1−ηk​μ)δk​+Lηk2​σ2/2, and 1−ηkμ≥01 - \eta_k\mu \ge 01−ηk​μ≥0 because ηk≤η0≤1/L≤1/μ\eta_k \le \eta_0 \le 1/L \le 1/\muηk​≤η0​≤1/L≤1/μ. We prove δk≤ν/(γ+k)\delta_k \le \nu/(\gamma + k)δk​≤ν/(γ+k) by induction. For k=0k = 0k=0 it holds because ν≥γδ0\nu \ge \gamma\delta_0ν≥γδ0​. If it holds for kkk, then

δk+1≤(1−βμγ+k)νγ+k+Lβ2σ22(γ+k)2=(γ+k−1) ν(γ+k)2−(βμ−1) ν−Lβ2σ2/2(γ+k)2.\delta_{k+1} \le \Big(1 - \frac{\beta\mu}{\gamma + k}\Big)\frac\nu{\gamma + k} + \frac{L\beta^2\sigma^2}{2(\gamma + k)^2} = \frac{(\gamma + k - 1)\,\nu}{(\gamma + k)^2} - \frac{(\beta\mu - 1)\,\nu - L\beta^2\sigma^2/2}{(\gamma + k)^2} .δk+1​≤(1−γ+kβμ​)γ+kν​+2(γ+k)2Lβ2σ2​=(γ+k)2(γ+k−1)ν​−(γ+k)2(βμ−1)ν−Lβ2σ2/2​.
(29)

The last fraction is non-negative by the definition of ν\nuν, and (γ+k−1)(γ+k+1)≤(γ+k)2(\gamma + k - 1)(\gamma + k + 1) \le (\gamma + k)^2(γ+k−1)(γ+k+1)≤(γ+k)2 gives γ+k−1(γ+k)2≤1γ+k+1\frac{\gamma + k - 1}{(\gamma + k)^2} \le \frac1{\gamma + k + 1}(γ+k)2γ+k−1​≤γ+k+11​. Hence δk+1≤ν/(γ+k+1)\delta_{k+1} \le \nu/(\gamma + k + 1)δk+1​≤ν/(γ+k+1). □\square□

With a decreasing step SGD converges to the minimum, at the sublinear rate O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k): the price of the noise is the loss of the linear rate, and, in the first iterations, a slower start (the step is smaller). Why would anyone accept a slower asymptotic rate than gradient descent? Because the cost of an iteration is BBB gradients instead of nnn, and because accuracy beyond the statistical error is wasted: the statistical error of a model fitted on nnn examples is of order 1/n1/n1/n in the loss for a linear model with a fixed number of parameters (each parameter costs of the order of σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n of prediction error, Section 6.2.1) and of order 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​ for the guarantees of Chapter 3, so an optimizer that has reached a suboptimality of that order has done its job; the O(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon)O(1/ε) iterations of SGD at that accuracy cost O(B/ε)O(B/\varepsilon)O(B/ε) gradients, independent of nnn, while GD pays O(nκlog⁡(1/ε))O(n\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))O(nκlog(1/ε)) (Bottou and Bousquet, 2008).

A last, cheap device is Polyak–Ruppert averaging: report not the last iterate but the average of the iterates, which cancels part of the noise around the minimum. We shall measure it below.

7.6.3 An experiment: SGD on the logistic regression¶

We compare, on the Breast Cancer problem of Section 7.3.4, the full-batch gradient with SGD, counting cost in epochs: one epoch is nnn per-example gradient evaluations, that is one pass over the data and the cost of a single full gradient, whatever the batch size. In practice the examples are not drawn with replacement at each iteration: one shuffles the training set at the start of each epoch and then sweeps through it in consecutive mini-batches (“random reshuffling”), so that every example is visited exactly once per epoch; the theory above is for sampling with replacement, and the behavior is very similar. The function sgd below runs SGD on any objective and records the suboptimality f(w)−f∗f(\mathbf{w}) - f^\astf(w)−f∗ at the end of every epoch; sgd_logistic applies it to the problem of Section 7.3.4. Its decreasing schedule ηk=η0/(1+k/τ)\eta_k = \eta_0/(1 + k/\tau)ηk​=η0​/(1+k/τ) has the form of Theorem 7.12 with β=η0τ\beta = \eta_0\tauβ=η0​τ and γ=τ\gamma = \tauγ=τ.

def sgd(obj, w0, n, batch, eta, epochs, f_star, decay=None, average=False, seed=SEED):
    """SGD with random reshuffling for an objective obj(w, idx) -> (f, gradient on the rows idx) of n examples.
    Returns the suboptimality f - f_star after each epoch and the last iterate.
    Step size eta_k = eta (constant) or eta / (1 + k / decay), k = number of updates so far.
    With average=True the suboptimality of the running mean of all the iterates is reported."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = w0.copy()
    w_avg, count, k = w.copy(), 0, 0
    gaps = np.empty(epochs)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = rng.permutation(n)
        for start in range(0, n, batch):
            idx = None if batch >= n else perm[start:start + batch]      # batch = n: the full gradient
            _, g = obj(w, idx=idx)
            w = w - (eta if decay is None else eta / (1 + k / decay)) * g
            k += 1
            count += 1
            w_avg += (w - w_avg) / count
        gaps[ep] = obj(w_avg if average else w)[0] - f_star
    return gaps, w


def sgd_logistic(batch, eta, epochs, decay=None, average=False, seed=SEED):
    return sgd(logistic_obj, np.zeros(d_b + 1), n_b, batch, eta, epochs, f_star_b, decay, average, seed)[0]


EPOCHS = 300
epochs_shown = [10, 50, 100, 200, 300]


def summarize(gaps):
    row = {f"epoch {e}": gaps[e - 1] for e in epochs_shown}
    row["mean of epochs 251-300"] = gaps[250:].mean()
    return row


runs_sgd = {}
rows = []
for eta in [1.0, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03]:
    with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
        runs_sgd[f"constant eta = {eta}"] = sgd_logistic(1, eta, EPOCHS)
    rows.append({"batch 1": f"constant eta = {eta}", **summarize(runs_sgd[f"constant eta = {eta}"])})
for eta0, tau in [(1.0, 5 * n_b), (0.3, 20 * n_b)]:
    key = f"decreasing, eta_0 = {eta0}, tau = {tau}"
    runs_sgd[key] = sgd_logistic(1, eta0, EPOCHS, decay=tau)
    rows.append({"batch 1": key, **summarize(runs_sgd[key])})
runs_sgd["averaged, eta = 0.3"] = sgd_logistic(1, 0.3, EPOCHS, average=True)
rows.append({"batch 1": "averaged iterates, constant eta = 0.3", **summarize(runs_sgd["averaged, eta = 0.3"])})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2e}"))

def figure_7_8():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.2))

    for key, color, label in [("constant eta = 0.3", VERMILION, r"constant $\eta = 0.3$"),

    ax.set(yscale="log", xlabel="epoch (one pass over the data)", ylabel=r"suboptimality $f(\mathbf{w}) - f^\ast$",
           title="SGD with batch size 1, Breast Cancer (one run, seed 42)", xlim=(1, EPOCHS), ylim=(1e-5, 60))
