figure_7_8()

Four observations, each of which is a statement of the theory.

  1. A constant step has a noise floor, and the floor falls with the step. After the transient, the suboptimality of the constant-step runs fluctuates around a level that depends on η\etaη: 8.3⋅10−28.3 \cdot 10^{-2}8.3⋅10−2 for η=0.3\eta = 0.3η=0.3, 8.6⋅10−38.6 \cdot 10^{-3}8.6⋅10−3 for η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1 and 5.3⋅10−45.3 \cdot 10^{-4}5.3⋅10−4 for η=0.03\eta = 0.03η=0.03 (the mean over epochs 251 to 300 of this single run; each epoch’s value is itself random, which is why the figure is so jagged). The floor falls faster than proportionally to η\etaη, which does not contradict Theorem 7.11: the theorem is an upper bound that uses the worst-case variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, while the actual per-example variance decreases as the iterate approaches the minimizer (Section 7.6.1). The step η=1\eta = 1η=1 is above the range η≤1/Lglob=0.30\eta \le 1/L_{\text{glob}} = 0.30η≤1/Lglob​=0.30 of the theorem and gives a floor of 0.55: it does not diverge, but it is useless.

  2. A decreasing step converges, but starts slower. With ηk=1/(1+k/2130)\eta_k = 1/(1 + k/2130)ηk​=1/(1+k/2130) the suboptimality is 5.1⋅10−25.1 \cdot 10^{-2}5.1⋅10−2 at epoch 10, when the best constant step already has 4.8⋅10−44.8 \cdot 10^{-4}4.8⋅10−4, and it keeps decreasing to 3.4⋅10−53.4 \cdot 10^{-5}3.4⋅10−5 at epoch 300 (mean over the last 50 epochs: 1.4⋅10−41.4 \cdot 10^{-4}1.4⋅10−4), below the floor of every constant step in the table. The crossover occurs after about 200 epochs. This is the usual compromise: a large step to move fast at the beginning, a small one to settle at the end.

  3. Averaging the iterates lowers the floor but does not remove it. For the constant step 0.3 the average of all the iterates has a suboptimality of 1.3⋅10−21.3 \cdot 10^{-2}1.3⋅10−2, six times lower than the last iterate (8.3⋅10−28.3 \cdot 10^{-2}8.3⋅10−2), and it plateaus there. In practice one averages only the last part of the run (“tail averaging”) or combines averaging with a smaller step.

  4. On this small problem SGD is not competitive. Full-batch gradient descent with the tuned step η=8\eta = 8η=8 reaches a suboptimality of 10-8 in 69 epochs (Section 7.3.4), and SGD has not reached 10-4 after 300. With n=426n = 426n=426 examples and a well-conditioned loss (κloc=24\kappa_{\text{loc}} = 24κloc​=24) a full gradient is cheap and the extra iterations of SGD buy nothing; SGD pays off when nnn is large (we measure this on Digits in Section 7.7.1), when moderate accuracy suffices, and when the data do not fit in memory.

The batch size controls the noise. By Proposition 7.10 and Theorem 7.11 the floor is proportional to η/B\eta/Bη/B, so multiplying BBB and η\etaη by the same factor should leave it unchanged (the linear scaling rule), while a larger batch at a fixed step should lower it. The next cell tests both statements with six runs, ordered by η/B\eta/Bη/B.

rows = []
for B, eta in [(64, 0.1), (64, 0.8), (8, 0.1), (1, 0.0125), (1, 0.1), (8, 0.8)]:
    with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
        gaps = sgd_logistic(B, eta, EPOCHS)
    rows.append({"batch": B, "eta": eta, "eta / B": eta / B, "epoch 10": gaps[9], "epoch 50": gaps[49],
                 "epoch 300": gaps[299], "mean of epochs 251-300": gaps[250:].mean()})
batch_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("eta / B")

At a fixed step η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1 the floor falls with the batch size (about 9⋅10−39 \cdot 10^{-3}9⋅10−3, 3⋅10−43 \cdot 10^{-4}3⋅10−4, 2⋅10−52 \cdot 10^{-5}2⋅10−5 for B=1,8,64B = 1, 8, 64B=1,8,64), but the early progress per epoch is slower for large batches, since an epoch contains fewer updates (4.5⋅10−34.5 \cdot 10^{-3}4.5⋅10−3 at epoch 10 for B=1B = 1B=1 against 2.9⋅10−22.9 \cdot 10^{-2}2.9⋅10−2 for B=64B = 64B=64). The floors are ordered like η/B\eta/Bη/B, as the theory predicts, and the three runs with η/B=0.0125\eta/B = 0.0125η/B=0.0125 have floors of the same order of magnitude (5⋅10−55 \cdot 10^{-5}5⋅10−5, 3⋅10−43 \cdot 10^{-4}3⋅10−4, 1.5⋅10−41.5 \cdot 10^{-4}1.5⋅10−4), although not equal: the rule is a rule of thumb that follows from an upper bound. In wall-clock time, on hardware that evaluates a batch of BBB examples in parallel (a GPU), a larger batch costs little more than a small one, which is the practical reason for the scaling rule; our sequential NumPy loops do not show this effect.

7.7 SGD in practice¶

7.7.1 Choosing the learning rate¶

Theory tells us that the step size must be below a ceiling of order 1/L1/L1/L and that the best value is a compromise between speed and noise; it does not tell us the number, because LLL is unknown and the useful constants are local. The practical recipe is a grid search on a logarithmic scale: run each candidate for a short, fixed budget (a few epochs), compare the training objective (the quantity being optimized, not the validation score), and keep the best, which is typically the largest value that does not diverge or oscillate. Schedules refine the picture: a constant step followed by a decay (a drop by a factor of 10 when progress stalls, a smooth cosine decay, or the 1/(1+k/τ)1/(1 + k/\tau)1/(1+k/τ) of Theorem 7.12), and often a short warm-up (a linear increase of the step over the first iterations) when the early gradients are large.

We run the experiment on the multi-class problem of Section 6.6: softmax regression on Digits (1,347 training images, 64 standardized pixels, ten classes, λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn) with C=3.16C = 3.16C=3.16, the value chosen by cross-validation in Chapter 6). The loss is smooth and strongly convex, the number of parameters is 650, and nnn is three times larger than for Breast Cancer. As before we compute the exact minimum f∗f^\astf∗ first (with L-BFGS), and we use the global smoothness bound L=σmax⁡2/(2n)+λL = \sigma_{\max}^2/(2n) + \lambdaL=σmax2​/(2n)+λ (the softmax Hessian is bounded by 12\frac1221​ of the feature Gram matrix) to express the step sizes as multiples of 1/L1/L1/L.

dg = load_digits()
Xg_tr, Xg_te, yg_tr, yg_te = train_test_split(dg.data, dg.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=dg.target)
scaler_g = StandardScaler().fit(Xg_tr)
Zg, Zg_te = scaler_g.transform(Xg_tr), scaler_g.transform(Xg_te)
n_g, d_g = Zg.shape
K_g = 10
Yg = np.eye(K_g)[yg_tr]
lam_g = 1 / (3.16 * n_g)                       # C = 3.16, as chosen by cross-validation in Chapter 6
print(f"Digits: {n_g} training images, {d_g} pixels, {K_g} classes, lambda = {lam_g:.2e}")


def softmax_obj(w, idx=None):
    """Mean cross-entropy + (lam/2)||W||^2 (intercepts not penalized) and its gradient; w = (W.ravel(), b)."""
    W, b = w[:K_g * d_g].reshape(K_g, d_g), w[K_g * d_g:]
    A, Y = (Zg, Yg) if idx is None else (Zg[idx], Yg[idx])
    S = A @ W.T + b
    logp = S - logsumexp(S, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    P = np.exp(logp)
    f = -np.mean(np.sum(Y * logp, axis=1)) + 0.5 * lam_g * np.sum(W**2)
    gW = (P - Y).T @ A / len(A) + lam_g * W
    gb = (P - Y).mean(axis=0)
    return f, np.r_[gW.ravel(), gb]


w0_g = np.zeros(K_g * d_g + K_g)
g_chk = np.random.default_rng(SEED).normal(size=w0_g.size) * 0.1
print(f"relative error of the analytic gradient: "
      f"{np.linalg.norm(softmax_obj(g_chk)[1] - central_difference(lambda w: softmax_obj(w)[0], g_chk)) / np.linalg.norm(softmax_obj(g_chk)[1]):.1e}")

res_g = minimize(softmax_obj, w0_g, jac=True, method="L-BFGS-B", options={"maxiter": 5000, "gtol": 1e-12, "ftol": 1e-16})
f_star_g, w_star_g = res_g.fun, res_g.x
L_g = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Zg.T @ Zg / n_g)[-1] / 2 + lam_g
accuracy_g = lambda w: np.mean((Zg_te @ w[:K_g * d_g].reshape(K_g, d_g).T + w[K_g * d_g:]).argmax(axis=1) == yg_te)
print(f"f* = {f_star_g:.8f} (L-BFGS, {res_g.nit} iterations), L = {L_g:.3f}, test accuracy of the exact minimizer: {accuracy_g(w_star_g):.4f}")

grid = [0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100]                 # step sizes, in units of 1/L
configs = {"full batch (GD)": n_g, "batch 128": 128, "batch 16": 16, "batch 1": 1}
EPOCHS_G = 30
results_g = {}
t0 = time.time()
for name, B in configs.items():
    for etaL in grid:
        with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
            results_g[(name, etaL)] = sgd(softmax_obj, w0_g, n_g, B, etaL / L_g, EPOCHS_G, f_star_g)
print(f"{len(results_g)} runs of {EPOCHS_G} epochs in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

best_g, rows = {}, []
for name in configs:
    cands = [(results_g[(name, e)][0][-1], e) for e in grid if np.isfinite(results_g[(name, e)][0][-1])]
    _, etaL = min(cands)

    best_g[name] = etaL

                 "test accuracy": accuracy_g(w)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))

# Figure 7.9 — the learning-rate grid, and the best run of each method
def figure_7_9():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0))
    colors = {"full batch (GD)": BLUE, "batch 128": GREEN, "batch 16": ORANGE, "batch 1": VERMILION}
    for name, color in colors.items():
        xs, ys = [], []
        for etaL in grid:
            g10 = results_g[(name, etaL)][0][9]
            if np.isfinite(g10) and g10 < 10:
                xs.append(etaL)
                ys.append(g10)
        axes[0].plot(xs, ys, "-o", color=color, lw=1.8, ms=5, mec="white", label=name)
        gaps = results_g[(name, best_g[name])][0]
        axes[1].plot(np.arange(1, EPOCHS_G + 1), gaps, color=color, lw=2, label=f"{name}, $\\eta L = {best_g[name]}$")
    axes[0].set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel=r"step size $\eta$ in units of $1/L$", ylim=(5e-3, 80),
                ylabel=r"suboptimality after 10 epochs", title="(a) the learning-rate grid")
    axes[1].set(yscale="log", xlabel="epoch", ylabel=r"suboptimality $f - f^\ast$", title="(b) the best run of each method")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
    axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_9()

Three facts stand out. First, each method has a U-shaped curve in η\etaη: too small a step makes no progress in 10 epochs, too large a step makes the iteration unstable and the points of the grid that diverged are missing from the plot. Second, the best step grows with the batch size, from 0.1/L0.1/L0.1/L for pure SGD through 1/L1/L1/L and 10/L10/L10/L for batches of 16 and 128 to 30/L30/L30/L for full-batch gradient descent, roughly in proportion to BBB (the scaling rule of Section 7.6.3); for the large batches these values are far above the 1/L1/L1/L of the theory, because LLL is the global bound and the curvature near the solution is smaller. Third, with the best step of each, the stochastic methods are ahead of full-batch GD per epoch: after 30 epochs the suboptimality is 0.0149 for GD and between 0.0018 and 0.0044 for SGD, and the test accuracies of the stochastic methods (0.969 to 0.971) are as close to that of the exact minimizer (0.973) as the evaluation on 450 images can resolve, while GD’s final iterate is a little behind (0.956). That is the regime in which SGD is worth using (compare with Breast Cancer, where nnn is small and the problem well conditioned): each epoch of SGD performs n/Bn/Bn/B updates instead of one, and the early iterations, when the gradient is large compared with the noise, are almost as good as full gradients at a fraction of the cost. L-BFGS needs 209 iterations to reach the exact minimum, that is 209 full gradients, more than the 30 epochs after which SGD is already within a suboptimality of 0.002 to 0.004.

7.7.2 Early stopping is implicit ridge regression¶

An iterative optimizer is a path in parameter space, and the model that we use is the point at which we stop. For gradient descent started at w0=0\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}w0​=0 on a least-squares problem, Theorem 7.3 describes that path exactly, and it is the same family of solutions as the ridge path of Section 6.3.2.

Proposition 7.13 (gradient descent as a spectral filter)

Let H=1nX⊤X=V diag(hj) V⊤≻0\mathbf{H} = \frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{V}\,\mathrm{diag}(h_j)\,\mathbf{V}^\top \succ 0H=n1​X⊤X=Vdiag(hj​)V⊤≻0, let w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ be the least-squares solution, and let gradient descent with 0<η≤1/L0 < \eta \le 1/L0<η≤1/L start from w0=0\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}w0​=0. Then

wk=V diag(φj(k)) V⊤w^,φj(k)=1−(1−ηhj)k,\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{V}\,\mathrm{diag}\big(\varphi_j(k)\big)\,\mathbf{V}^\top\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \qquad \varphi_j(k) = 1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^k,wk​=Vdiag(φj​(k))V⊤w^,φj​(k)=1−(1−ηhj​)k,
(30)

whereas the ridge estimator with penalty λ\lambdaλ (the objective 12n∥y−Xw∥2+λ2∥w∥2\frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^22n1​∥y−Xw∥2+2λ​∥w∥2) is w^λ=V diag(rj(λ))V⊤w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda = \mathbf{V}\,\mathrm{diag}\big(r_j(\lambda)\big)\mathbf{V}^\top\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^λ​=Vdiag(rj​(λ))V⊤w^ with rj(λ)=hj/(hj+λ)r_j(\lambda) = h_j/(h_j + \lambda)rj​(λ)=hj​/(hj​+λ). If λ=1/(ηk)\lambda = 1/(\eta k)λ=1/(ηk), then for every direction jjj

rj(λ)≤φj(k)≤2 rj(λ).r_j(\lambda) \le \varphi_j(k) \le 2\,r_j(\lambda).rj​(λ)≤φj​(k)≤2rj​(λ).
(31)

Both filters keep the directions of large hjh_jhj​ (large curvature, where the data are informative) and suppress those of small hjh_jhj​; the number of steps plays the role of 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ.

Proof

The first formula is Theorem 7.3 with w0=0\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}w0​=0 (w0−w∗=−w^\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast = -\hat{\mathbf{w}}w0​−w∗=−w^), the second is the ridge formula of Section 6.3.2. Put x=ηhj∈(0,1]x = \eta h_j \in (0, 1]x=ηhj​∈(0,1] and t=kx=hj/λt = kx = h_j/\lambdat=kx=hj​/λ, so that rj=t/(1+t)r_j = t/(1 + t)rj​=t/(1+t). Lower bound: (1−x)k≤e−kx=e−t≤1/(1+t)(1 - x)^k \le e^{-kx} = e^{-t} \le 1/(1 + t)(1−x)k≤e−kx=e−t≤1/(1+t), hence φj=1−(1−x)k≥1−1/(1+t)=t/(1+t)\varphi_j = 1 - (1 - x)^k \ge 1 - 1/(1 + t) = t/(1 + t)φj​=1−(1−x)k≥1−1/(1+t)=t/(1+t). Upper bound: by Bernoulli’s inequality (1−x)k≥1−kx(1 - x)^k \ge 1 - kx(1−x)k≥1−kx, so φj≤min⁡{1,t}\varphi_j \le \min\{1, t\}φj​≤min{1,t}; and min⁡{1,t}≤2t/(1+t)\min\{1, t\} \le 2t/(1 + t)min{1,t}≤2t/(1+t) (for t≤1t \le 1t≤1 because 1+t≤21 + t \le 21+t≤2, for t≥1t \ge 1t≥1 because 2t/(1+t)≥12t/(1 + t) \ge 12t/(1+t)≥1). □\square□

The sandwich is not an equality, so early-stopped GD is not exactly a ridge estimator, but it is within a factor 2 in every direction, and the two paths are very close in practice. We verify it on the Diabetes problem of Section 7.3.2: along the gradient-descent path (with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L) and along the ridge path with λ=1/(ηk)\lambda = 1/(\eta k)λ=1/(ηk) we compute the exact solution after kkk steps (by the formula, which is exact for a quadratic) and the test error on the 111 held-out patients.

h_d, V_d = np.linalg.eigh(H_d)
a_d = V_d.T @ w_star_d                                       # least-squares solution in the eigenbasis
eta_es = 1 / L_d


def w_gd(k):
    return V_d @ ((1 - (1 - eta_es * h_d) ** k) * a_d)


def w_ridge(lam):
    return V_d @ (h_d / (h_d + lam) * a_d)


test_mse = lambda w: np.mean((yd_te - yd_mean - Zd_te @ w) ** 2)
ks_es = np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, 5, 120)).astype(np.int64))
mse_gd = np.array([test_mse(w_gd(k)) for k in ks_es])
mse_rd = np.array([test_mse(w_ridge(1 / (eta_es * k))) for k in ks_es])
mse_ols = test_mse(w_star_d)
i_gd, i_rd = mse_gd.argmin(), mse_rd.argmin()
print(f"least squares (the end of both paths): test MSE {mse_ols:.1f}")
print(f"best early-stopped GD: k = {ks_es[i_gd]}, test MSE {mse_gd[i_gd]:.1f}")
print(f"best ridge on the same grid: lambda = 1/(eta k) = {1 / (eta_es * ks_es[i_rd]):.3f}, test MSE {mse_rd[i_rd]:.1f}")

phi = 1 - (1 - eta_es * h_d[None, :]) ** ks_es[:, None]
rr = h_d[None, :] / (h_d[None, :] + 1 / (eta_es * ks_es[:, None]))
print(f"ratio of the GD filter to the ridge filter, over all directions and all k: from {(phi / rr).min():.3f} to {(phi / rr).max():.3f} "
      f"(Proposition 7.13: between 1 and 2)")
for k in (100, 1000, 10000):
    wg, wr = w_gd(k), w_ridge(1 / (eta_es * k))
    print(f"k = {k:>5}: ||w_GD|| = {np.linalg.norm(wg):6.1f}, ||w_ridge|| = {np.linalg.norm(wr):6.1f}, "

def figure_7_10():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0))
    ax = axes[0]

    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper right")
    ax = axes[1]
    for k, color in [(100, BLUE), (1000, VERMILION)]:
        ax.plot(h_d, 1 - (1 - eta_es * h_d) ** k, "-o", color=color, lw=1.8, ms=5, mec="white", label=f"gradient descent, $k = {k}$")
        ax.plot(h_d, h_d / (h_d + 1 / (eta_es * k)), "--s", color=color, lw=1.2, ms=4, mec="white", label=rf"ridge, $\lambda = 1/(\eta k)$, $k = {k}$")
    ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel=r"eigenvalue $h_j$ of the Hessian", ylabel="filter factor",
           title="(b) fraction of each direction retained")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_10()

The two test-error curves are almost the same: a minimum slightly below the least-squares error (1.2%1.2\%1.2% lower for early stopping at k=7k = 7k=7, 1.4%1.4\%1.4% for ridge, differences of about one percent, well within the noise of an evaluation on 111 test patients: in Section 6.3.4 ridge gained 7 points out of 2848 on this very split, and nothing on average over many splits) and a return to the least-squares value as k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞. The ratio of the two filters, computed over all ten directions and all the iteration counts of the grid, lies between 1.000 and 2.000: both bounds of Proposition 7.13 are attained (the upper one at k=1k = 1k=1 in the steepest direction, where gradient descent with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L removes the whole error and ridge only half). The weights differ by 4.5%4.5\%4.5%, 20%20\%20% and 3.3%3.3\%3.3% at k=100k = 100k=100, 103 and 104; the paths are the same family, not the same curve.

Early stopping regularizes in the metric of the parametrization, because the filter acts on the eigenvectors of the Hessian of the problem as it is posed. The same kkk means different things in different units. The next cell stops gradient descent after the same numbers of iterations on the standardized and on the raw Diabetes features, from w0=0\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}w0​=0, again exactly by the formula of Theorem 7.3.

h_raw, V_raw = np.linalg.eigh(H_raw)
w_ols_raw = np.linalg.solve(H_raw, b_raw)
a_raw = V_raw.T @ w_ols_raw
eta_raw = 1 / h_raw[-1]
Xte_c = Xd_te - Xd_tr.mean(axis=0)
test_mse_raw = lambda w: np.mean((yd_te - yd_mean - Xte_c @ w) ** 2)
rows = []
for k in [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    w_raw_k = V_raw @ ((1 - (1 - eta_raw * h_raw) ** k) * a_raw)
    rows.append({"k": k, "test MSE, standardized": test_mse(w_gd(k)), "test MSE, raw units": test_mse_raw(w_raw_k)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"))
print(f"(least squares: {mse_ols:.1f}; the variance of the test targets around the training mean: {np.mean((yd_te - yd_mean) ** 2):.1f})")
      k  test MSE, standardized  test MSE, raw units
      1                  3151.5               4759.9
     10                  2819.4               3718.8
    100                  2843.4               3132.3
   1000                  2846.6               3049.0
  10000                  2848.3               2971.9
 100000                  2848.3               2873.6
1000000                  2848.3               2848.3
(least squares: 2848.3; the variance of the test targets around the training mean: 5607.2)

On the standardized features the path has a sweet spot around k=10k = 10k=10 (test MSE 2819, below the least-squares 2848) and is at the end of its journey after 103 steps. In raw units the path is monotone and never beats least squares: its test error falls from 4760 after one step to 3049 after a thousand (7%7\%7% above least squares) and only reaches 2848 after about a million steps. Here early stopping hurts, because the filter shrinks the directions that have small variance in the raw units, which are not the directions where the data are uninformative. The raw problem is not “more regularized”; it is regularized in the wrong geometry. This is one more reason to standardize (Section 7.4), and a warning that a number of epochs found for one parametrization does not transfer to another.

7.7.3 Gradient descent chooses the maximum-margin classifier¶

Section 6.4.4 left an open question: on separable data the logistic regression without a penalty has no minimizer, the weights diverge, and “the unpenalized fit is determined by the stopping rule”. We can now say what the stopping rule does. Take labels yi∈{−1,+1}y_i \in \{-1, +1\}yi​∈{−1,+1}, features x~i\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_ix~i​ (with a constant coordinate for the intercept), and suppose that some w\mathbf{w}w has yiw⊤x~i>0y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i > 0yi​w⊤x~i​>0 for all iii. The hard-margin direction is the solution of

w^=arg⁡min⁡w ∥w∥subject toyi w⊤x~i≥1  for all i,\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\ \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i\,\mathbf{w}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i \ge 1\ \text{ for all } i,w^=argwmin​ ∥w∥subject toyi​w⊤x~i​≥1  for all i,
(32)

the separating hyperplane with the largest margin, the object of Chapter 8.

Theorem 7.14 (implicit bias of gradient descent; Soudry et al., 2018; stated without proof)

For linearly separable data, gradient descent on the unpenalized logistic loss with a constant step η<2/L\eta < 2/Lη<2/L, from any starting point, satisfies f(wk)→0f(\mathbf{w}_k) \to 0f(wk​)→0, ∥wk∥→∞\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert \to \infty∥wk​∥→∞, and

wk∥wk∥⟶w^∥w^∥,wk=w^ ln⁡k+ρk,\frac{\mathbf{w}_k}{\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert} \longrightarrow \frac{\hat{\mathbf{w}}}{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert}, \qquad \mathbf{w}_k = \hat{\mathbf{w}}\,\ln k + \boldsymbol\rho_k,∥wk​∥wk​​⟶∥w^∥w^​,wk​=w^lnk+ρk​,
(33)

where the correction ρk\boldsymbol\rho_kρk​ grows much more slowly than ln⁡k\ln klnk (it is bounded when the support vectors span the data). The direction converges only at the rate O(1/ln⁡k)O(1/\ln k)O(1/lnk).

In words: the logistic loss decreases forever by growing the weights, the size of wk\mathbf{w}_kwk​ is set by the number of iterations (logarithmically), and the direction converges, among all the separating directions, to the one with the largest margin. Early stopping then chooses a size, hence how confident the probabilities are, while the direction is already that of the support vector machine. Worked example 7.2 was the one-dimensional case: wkw_kwk​ grows like log⁡k\log klogk.

We check the theorem on the two Iris classes of Section 6.4.4 (setosa against versicolor, petal length and width, standardized), which are separable. We append the constant column and compute the hard-margin direction in the augmented space with LinearSVC with a very large CCC, without intercept: that is the optimization problem above (we use it here as a black box, and Chapter 8 explains it). Then we run gradient descent with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L for one million iterations and compare.

iris = load_iris()
mask = iris.target < 2
Zi = StandardScaler().fit_transform(iris.data[mask][:, [2, 3]])
yi = iris.target[mask].astype(float)                          # 0 = setosa, 1 = versicolor
Ai = np.c_[np.ones(len(yi)), Zi]                               # augmented features
si = 2 * yi - 1                                                # labels in {-1, +1}

svm = LinearSVC(C=1e6, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, dual=True, max_iter=2_000_000, tol=1e-10).fit(Ai, yi)
w_hat = svm.coef_.ravel()
margins = si * (Ai @ w_hat)
print(f"hard-margin direction (augmented space): {np.round(w_hat, 4)}, ||w_hat|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_hat):.4f}")
print(f"constraints that are active (margin = 1): examples {np.flatnonzero(margins < 1 + 1e-6)}; "
      f"largest geometric margin = 1/||w_hat|| = {1 / np.linalg.norm(w_hat):.4f}")

L_i = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Ai.T @ Ai / len(yi))[-1] / 4
w_i = np.zeros(3)
checkpoints = {10, 100, 1000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000}
rows, path_i = [], []
log_ks = set(np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, 6, 61)).astype(int)))
for k in range(1, 1_000_001):
    w_i = w_i - (1 / L_i) * (Ai.T @ (expit(Ai @ w_i) - yi)) / len(yi)
    if k in log_ks:
        path_i.append((k, w_i.copy()))
    if k in checkpoints:
        cos = w_i @ w_hat / (np.linalg.norm(w_i) * np.linalg.norm(w_hat))
        rows.append({"k": k, "||w_k||": np.linalg.norm(w_i), "angle to w_hat (degrees)": np.degrees(np.arccos(min(1.0, cos))),
                     "geometric margin": (si * (Ai @ w_i)).min() / np.linalg.norm(w_i),
                     "training loss": np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, -si * (Ai @ w_i)))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))
norms = [r["||w_k||"] for r in rows]
print(f"increase of ||w_k|| per decade of k: {np.round(np.diff(norms), 2)}; the theorem predicts ||w_hat|| ln(10) = {np.linalg.norm(w_hat) * np.log(10):.2f}")

def figure_7_11():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0))
    ax = axes[0]
    for cls, color, marker, label in [(0, BLUE, "o", "setosa"), (1, ORANGE, "s", "versicolor")]:

    ax.plot(kk, nn, color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$\|\mathbf{w}_k\|$ (measured)")
    ref = np.linalg.norm(w_hat) * np.log(kk / 1000) + nn[list(kk).index(1000)]
    ax.plot(kk, ref, color=VERMILION, lw=1.5, ls="--", label=r"$\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}\|\,\ln k$, anchored at $k = 10^3$")
    ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="iteration $k$", ylabel=r"norm of the weights", title="(b) the weights grow like $\\ln k$")

figure_7_11()

The hard-margin solution has two active constraints (two support vectors), a geometric margin of 0.646 and a norm of 1.549. After 103 steps the gradient-descent direction is within 2.1∘2.1^\circ2.1∘ of it and its margin is 96%96\%96% of the maximum; after 106 steps the margin is 99%99\%99% of the maximum (0.640 against 0.646). The norm of the weights grows like the theorem says: by about 2.8, 3.1 and 3.3 per decade of iterations, approaching ∥w^∥ln⁡10=3.57\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}\|\ln 10 = 3.57∥w^∥ln10=3.57, while the training loss falls from 3.5⋅10−23.5 \cdot 10^{-2}3.5⋅10−2 to 10-6: the loss is already below 10-3 after a thousand steps, but the iterates keep moving, slowly, toward the max-margin direction. One detail deserves honesty: the angle is not monotone, it falls to 2.1∘2.1^\circ2.1∘ at k=103k = 10^3k=103 and then rises slowly to 3.0∘3.0^\circ3.0∘ at k=106k = 10^6k=106. The theorem guarantees convergence of the direction, with a correction ρk\boldsymbol\rho_kρk​ that is bounded only when the support vectors span the data, and here two support vectors cannot span the three-dimensional augmented space; this is consistent with a slowly growing correction, but we have not tested that explanation. The practical message is the one of the theorem: the direction converges extremely slowly (as 1/ln⁡k1/\ln k1/lnk), and nobody runs gradient descent long enough to reach it exactly, but the region in which early-stopped solutions lie is close to the support vector machine, and, in this experiment, very close after a thousand steps.

7.8 Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam¶

Different coordinates of a model can have gradients of very different sizes (the raw Diabetes problem is an example), and in sparse problems some coordinates are updated rarely. Adaptive methods give each coordinate its own step size, built from the history of its gradients. All use the elementwise square g2\mathbf{g}^2g2 of the gradient.

  • AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan and Singer, 2011) accumulates Gk=Gk−1+gk2\mathbf{G}_k = \mathbf{G}_{k-1} + \mathbf{g}_k^2Gk​=Gk−1​+gk2​ and moves by −η gk/(Gk+ε)-\eta\,\mathbf{g}_k/(\sqrt{\mathbf{G}_k} + \varepsilon)−ηgk​/(Gk​​+ε): coordinates with large past gradients get small steps.

  • RMSprop (Hinton, 2012) replaces the sum by a moving average, vk=ρvk−1+(1−ρ)gk2\mathbf{v}_k = \rho\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + (1 - \rho)\mathbf{g}_k^2vk​=ρvk−1​+(1−ρ)gk2​, so that the memory is finite and the steps do not shrink to zero.

  • Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) adds momentum and a correction for the zero initialization of the averages:

    mk=β1mk−1+(1−β1)gk,vk=β2vk−1+(1−β2)gk2,wk+1=wk−η mk/(1−β1k)vk/(1−β2k)+ε,\mathbf{m}_k = \beta_1\mathbf{m}_{k-1} + (1 - \beta_1)\mathbf{g}_k, \quad \mathbf{v}_k = \beta_2\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + (1 - \beta_2)\mathbf{g}_k^2, \quad \mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\,\frac{\mathbf{m}_k/(1 - \beta_1^k)}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_k/(1 - \beta_2^k)} + \varepsilon},mk​=β1​mk−1​+(1−β1​)gk​,vk​=β2​vk−1​+(1−β2​)gk2​,wk+1​=wk​−ηvk​/(1−β2k​)​+εmk​/(1−β1k​)​,
    (34)

    with the usual defaults β1=0.9\beta_1 = 0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_2 = 0.999β2​=0.999, ε=10−8\varepsilon = 10^{-8}ε=10−8.

In the language of Section 7.4, these methods build a diagonal preconditioner from the gradient history, adapted at run time instead of fixed by the units of the features. Their step size is no longer in units of 1/L1/L1/L: the coordinate-wise move has size of order η\etaη whatever the scale of the gradient, which is why η\etaη for Adam is typically between 10-4 and 10-1 in the units of the parameters.

The next experiment is a comparison on a deterministic problem, with full gradients, so that only the update rule matters: Diabetes least squares in raw units (where the diagonal rescaling matters most) and standardized. For AdaGrad and Adam the step size η\etaη is chosen from a logarithmic grid by the final suboptimality after 3,0003{,}0003,000 iterations, that is with hindsight, which is favorable to them; gradient descent uses η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L. The numbers describe this problem and this tuning protocol, not a general ranking.

def adaptive_run(grad, record, w0, kind, eta, iters, eps=1e-8, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999):
    w = w0.copy()
    m, v, out = np.zeros_like(w), np.zeros_like(w), np.empty(iters)
    for k in range(1, iters + 1):
        out[k - 1] = record(w)
        g = grad(w)
        if kind == "adagrad":
            v += g**2
            w = w - eta * g / (np.sqrt(v) + eps)
        else:                                                    # Adam
            m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g
            v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2
            w = w - eta * (m / (1 - beta1**k)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - beta2**k)) + eps)
    return out


ITERS_A = 3000
problems = {"raw units": (H_raw, b_raw), "standardized": (H_d, b_d)}
curves_a, rows = {}, []
for pname, (H, b) in problems.items():
    ws = np.linalg.solve(H, b)
    grad_q = lambda w, H=H, b=b: H @ w - b
    rec_q = lambda w, H=H, ws=ws: 0.5 * (w - ws) @ H @ (w - ws)
    L_q = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)[-1]
    runs = {"gradient descent": (1 / L_q, momentum_run(grad_q, rec_q, np.zeros(10), 1 / L_q, lambda k: 0.0, ITERS_A, "hb"))}
    for kind, eta_grid in [("adagrad", [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10]), ("adam", [0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10])]:
        cands = []
        for eta in eta_grid:
            c = adaptive_run(grad_q, rec_q, np.zeros(10), kind, eta, ITERS_A)
            if np.isfinite(c[-1]):
                cands.append((c[-1], eta, c))
        _, eta_best, c_best = min(cands, key=lambda t: t[0])
        runs["AdaGrad" if kind == "adagrad" else "Adam"] = (eta_best, c_best)
    curves_a[pname] = runs
    for name, (eta, c) in runs.items():
        rows.append({"problem": pname, "method": name, "eta": eta, **{f"gap, k = {k}": max(c[k - 1], 0.0) for k in (10, 100, 1000, 3000)}})
print(f"initial suboptimality: raw {curves_a['raw units']['gradient descent'][1][0]:.0f}, "
      f"standardized {curves_a['standardized']['gradient descent'][1][0]:.0f}")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
c_adam = curves_a["raw units"]["Adam"][1]
print(f"Adam on raw units: smallest value {c_adam.min():.1e}, then the largest suboptimality between k = 1200 and 3000 is {c_adam[1199:].max():.1e}")

standardized gradient descent    0.255         19.9          9.45          0.127       8.71e-06

def figure_7_12():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0), sharey=True)
    for ax, pname in zip(axes, problems):

figure_7_12()

On raw units, gradient descent has removed only 94%94\%94% of the initial suboptimality (1569→861569 \to 861569→86) after 3,0003{,}0003,000 iterations, while AdaGrad reaches 0.15 and Adam 10-14 (machine precision): the per-coordinate scaling does for the units what the standardization of Section 7.4 does by hand, since the diagonal rescaling brings κ\kappaκ from 7.4⋅1047.4 \cdot 10^47.4⋅104 to 418. On the standardized problem there is nothing left for a diagonal rescaling to fix, and gradient descent and AdaGrad are close (8.7⋅10−68.7 \cdot 10^{-6}8.7⋅10−6 against 4.8⋅10−74.8 \cdot 10^{-7}4.8⋅10−7 at k=3000k = 3000k=3000); Adam is much faster at k=1000k = 1000k=1000 (8.5⋅10−48.5 \cdot 10^{-4}8.5⋅10−4 against 0.13), but note that it contains momentum, and the heavy ball of Section 7.5 is also far faster than gradient descent on this problem. Two warnings are visible in the table. Adam’s first iterations overshoot: its suboptimality after ten iterations is 6,7506{,}7506,750 on the raw problem, four times the initial value, because each coordinate moves by about η\etaη per step whatever the size of its gradient. On the raw problem there is a second symptom: after Adam has reached machine precision (a suboptimality of 4⋅10−284 \cdot 10^{-28}4⋅10−28 at its best), the suboptimality jumps back up in isolated spikes, the largest of about 3⋅1033 \cdot 10^{3}3⋅103 between k=1200k = 1200k=1200 and k=3000k = 3000k=3000, because the second-moment average of a gradient that has become tiny decays and the normalized step ηm^/v^\eta\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}ηm^/v^​ stops being small; the spikes are visible in Figure 7.12. And we tuned η\etaη with hindsight for both adaptive methods. In the stochastic setting, where Adam is mostly used, there is no equivalent of the contraction of Theorem 7.3; Adam can fail to converge even on convex problems with a constant β2\beta_2β2​ (Reddi, Kale and Kumar, 2018), and in practice it is run with a decaying step and a short warm-up. The rule of thumb that survives is modest: adaptive methods are less sensitive to the scale of the features and of the gradients, they are not a substitute for standardizing the inputs, and they do not remove the need to tune η\etaη.

7.9 Beyond convexity: saddles and many minima¶

Everything above rested on convexity: every critical point of a convex function is a global minimizer, and gradient descent finds it. The models of the next chapters are convex (support vector machines, Chapter 8, and the lasso of Chapter 10), but the neural networks of Part IV are not, and it is worth seeing now, on two small functions, what changes. Both functions are constructed, not data.

At a critical point ∇f(w)=0\nabla f(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}∇f(w)=0 the eigenvalues of the Hessian tell what kind of point it is: all positive, a local minimum; all negative, a local maximum; some positive and some negative, a saddle point. Gradient descent is attracted to minima and repelled by maxima, but a saddle is attractive along the directions of positive curvature and repulsive along those of negative curvature, so the iteration approaches it and then, unless it is exactly on the attractive manifold, leaves along the repulsive direction. The test case is f(x,y)=x44−x22+y22f(x, y) = \frac{x^4}4 - \frac{x^2}2 + \frac{y^2}2f(x,y)=4x4​−2x2​+2y2​, with a saddle at the origin (Hessian diag(−1,1)\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)diag(−1,1)) and two minima at (±1,0)(\pm 1, 0)(±1,0) (Hessian diag(2,1)\mathrm{diag}(2, 1)diag(2,1)). Near the origin the xxx-coordinate evolves as xk+1=xk(1+η−ηxk2)≈(1+η)xkx_{k+1} = x_k(1 + \eta - \eta x_k^2) \approx (1 + \eta)x_kxk+1​=xk​(1+η−ηxk2​)≈(1+η)xk​: it grows geometrically at rate 1+η∣λmin⁡∣1 + \eta\lvert\lambda_{\min}\rvert1+η∣λmin​∣, so starting at distance ∣x0∣\lvert x_0\rvert∣x0​∣ from the saddle the escape takes about ln⁡(1/∣x0∣)/ln⁡(1+η)\ln(1/\lvert x_0\rvert)/\ln(1 + \eta)ln(1/∣x0​∣)/ln(1+η) iterations, plus the time needed to cross the nonlinear region. If x0x_0x0​ is exactly zero, however, the iteration stays on the line x=0x = 0x=0 and converges to the saddle.

eta_s = 0.1
rows = []
for x0 in [1e-2, 1e-6, 1e-12, 0.0]:
    p = np.array([x0, 1.0])
    hit = None
    for k in range(1, 5001):
        p = p - eta_s * np.array([p[0] ** 3 - p[0], p[1]])        # gradient of x^4/4 - x^2/2 + y^2/2
        if abs(abs(p[0]) - 1) < 1e-3:
            hit = k
            break
    est = np.log(1 / x0) / np.log(1 + eta_s) if x0 > 0 else np.inf
    rows.append({"x0": x0, "iterations to reach a minimum": hit if hit else "never (5000 run)",
                 "linearized estimate": est, "difference": (hit - est) if hit else np.nan})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
print(f"at the exact saddle start, the final point after 5000 steps is {p.round(6)}")
   x0 iterations to reach a minimum  linearized estimate  difference
 0.01                            77                 48.3        28.7
1e-06                           173                  145          28
1e-12                           318                  290        28.1
    0              never (5000 run)                  inf         NaN
at the exact saddle start, the final point after 5000 steps is [0. 0.]

The measured escape times, 77, 173 and 318 iterations, exceed the linearized estimates by almost the same amount (28 to 29 iterations), the time of the nonlinear crossing, which does not depend on x0x_0x0​. A starting point that is 10-12 away from the saddle needs only four times as many steps as one that is 10-2 away: a saddle is not a trap for gradient descent, except for the single starting point that sits exactly on its stable manifold. This is a general fact (“gradient descent almost surely avoids strict saddle points”, Lee et al., 2016), and in SGD the noise of the gradient moves the iterate off the stable manifold by itself, which is one of the reasons why SGD works better than the theory of Section 7.6 would lead one to expect on non-convex problems.

The second difficulty is that there may be several local minima, and which one gradient descent finds depends on where it starts. The Himmelblau function f(x,y)=(x2+y−11)2+(x+y2−7)2f(x, y) = (x^2 + y - 11)^2 + (x + y^2 - 7)^2f(x,y)=(x2+y−11)2+(x+y2−7)2, a classical test function, has four minima, all with f=0f = 0f=0. We start gradient descent from every point of a 201×201201 \times 201201×201 grid on [−5,5]2[-5, 5]^2[−5,5]2 and record the minimum it reaches.

def himmelblau_grad(P):
    x, y = P[..., 0], P[..., 1]
    return np.stack([4 * x * (x**2 + y - 11) + 2 * (x + y**2 - 7), 2 * (x**2 + y - 11) + 4 * y * (x + y**2 - 7)], axis=-1)


minima = np.array([[3.0, 2.0], [-2.805118, 3.131312], [-3.779310, -3.283186], [3.584428, -1.848126]])
print("largest gradient component at the four known minima:", np.abs(himmelblau_grad(minima)).max().round(5))
gx = np.linspace(-5, 5, 201)
P0 = np.stack(np.meshgrid(gx, gx), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2)
P = P0.copy()
for _ in range(3000):
    P = P - 0.005 * himmelblau_grad(P)
dist = np.linalg.norm(P[:, None, :] - minima[None], axis=2)
basin = dist.argmin(axis=1)
converged = dist.min(axis=1) < 1e-2
print(f"starting points that converge to a minimum: {converged.mean():.3f}")
print("share of the starting points that reach each minimum:", np.round([(basin[converged] == i).mean() for i in range(4)], 3))
largest gradient component at the four known minima: 4e-05

starting points that converge to a minimum: 1.000
share of the starting points that reach each minimum: [0.256 0.26  0.237 0.247]

# Figure 7.13 — a saddle point and four basins of attraction (constructed functions)
def figure_7_13():
    from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.2))
    ax = axes[0]
    g1, g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.7, 1.7, 300), np.linspace(-1.3, 1.3, 300))
    ax.contour(g1, g2, g1**4 / 4 - g1**2 / 2 + g2**2 / 2, levels=np.linspace(-0.2, 1.4, 12), colors="0.7", linewidths=0.8)
    for x0, color, lab in [(0.01, BLUE, r"$x_0 = +10^{-2}$"), (-0.01, ORANGE, r"$x_0 = -10^{-2}$"), (0.0, VERMILION, r"$x_0 = 0$ (exactly)")]:
        p = np.array([x0, 1.0])
        path = [p]
        for _ in range(160):
            p = p - eta_s * np.array([p[0] ** 3 - p[0], p[1]])
            path.append(p)
        path = np.array(path)
        ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "-", color=color, lw=1.8, label=lab)
        ax.plot(*path[0], "o", color=color, ms=5, mec="white")
    ax.plot([0], [0], "x", color="k", ms=9, mew=2)
    ax.plot([-1, 1], [0, 0], "*", color="k", ms=11)
    ax.set(xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", title="(a) the saddle at the origin ($\\times$), two minima ($\\star$)")
    ax.legend(frameon=True, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor="none", fontsize=8, loc="lower center", ncol=1)
    ax = axes[1]
    cmap = ListedColormap([BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, PURPLE])
    ax.imshow(basin.reshape(201, 201), origin="lower", extent=(-5, 5, -5, 5), cmap=cmap, alpha=0.55, interpolation="nearest")
    G1, G2 = np.meshgrid(gx, gx)
    ax.contour(G1, G2, (G1**2 + G2 - 11) ** 2 + (G1 + G2**2 - 7) ** 2, levels=[5, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400], colors="0.35", linewidths=0.6)
    ax.plot(minima[:, 0], minima[:, 1], "*", color="k", ms=12, mec="white")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_0$", ylabel="$y_0$", title="(b) which minimum gradient descent reaches")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_13()

The four basins, each reached from about a quarter of the starting points (25.6%25.6\%25.6%, 26.0%26.0\%26.0%, 23.7%23.7\%23.7% and 24.7%24.7\%24.7%), are interleaved, with boundaries that wind around the saddles between the minima: a small change of the starting point can change the answer. For this function the four minima are equally good (f=0f = 0f=0), but in general they are not, and the quality of the solution then depends on the initialization and on the path: this is the reason why the random seed matters for neural networks, and why the chapters on deep networks (Chapters 14 and 15) pay so much attention to initialization.

7.10 Choosing an optimizer¶

We close the chapter by putting side by side what the experiments measured. The first table reports, for the logistic regression of Section 7.3.4 (426 examples, 31 parameters, local condition number 24), the number of evaluations of the gradient needed to bring the suboptimality below 10-8. It is a cost in gradients (each is a pass over the data, of the order of npn pnp operations); Newton’s method needs 7 steps, each of which also forms and solves with the Hessian.

cost_rows = [
    ("gradient descent, eta = 1/L_glob = 0.30", iterations_to(gd_runs["1/L_glob = 0.30"]), "no tuning, safe by the theory"),
    ("gradient descent, eta = 8.7 (largest stable constant step)", iterations_to(gd_runs["8.7"]), "needs the unknown local L"),
    ("gradient descent with backtracking", len(gaps_bt) - 1, f"plus {n_func_bt - len(gaps_bt)} extra function evaluations"),
    ("Nesterov (strongly convex version)", iterations_to(curves_b["Nesterov, strongly convex version"]), "needs mu and L"),
    ("heavy ball, beta = 0.9", iterations_to(curves_b["heavy ball, beta = 0.9"]), "beta tuned by hand"),
    ("L-BFGS", int(hist[k_lb, 1]), "memory of a few gradient pairs"),
    ("Newton", 7, "7 Hessians and 7 linear solves"),
]
print(pd.DataFrame(cost_rows, columns=["method", "gradient evaluations to gap < 1e-8", "remark"]).to_string(index=False))
print(f"SGD, batch size 1, best constant step of the grid: suboptimality after {EPOCHS} epochs "
      f"(= {EPOCHS} gradient-equivalents): {runs_sgd['constant eta = 0.03'][-1]:.1e}")

gradient descent, eta = 8.7 (largest stable constant step)                                  65           needs the unknown local L

The same ordering is not universal: it depends on nnn, on the number of parameters ppp, on the conditioning and on the accuracy required. The guide below summarizes what the theory of this chapter and the experiments suggest.

MethodCost per iterationExtra memoryConvergence (smooth convex)Use it when
Gradient descentone full gradient, O(np)O(np)O(np)noneO(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k); linear with rate 1−1/κ1 - 1/\kappa1−1/κ if strongly convexthe problem is small and well conditioned, or as a baseline
Momentum / Nesterovone full gradientone vectorO(1/k2)O(1/k^2)O(1/k2); linear with 1−1/κ1 - 1/\sqrt\kappa1−1/κ​the problem is ill conditioned and only gradients are available
L-BFGSone full gradient and a few vector productsa few gradient pairsmuch faster in practice, no simple ratesmooth objective, up to millions of parameters, full data in memory (the default of LogisticRegression)
Newtongradient, Hessian, and a solve: O(np2+p3)O(np^2 + p^3)O(np2+p3)p2p^2p2quadratic near the solutionppp is at most a few thousand and the Hessian is available
SGD (mini-batch)BBB per-example gradients, O(Bp)O(Bp)O(Bp)nonenoise floor ∝η/B\propto\eta/B∝η/B; O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) with decreasing stepnnn is large or the data arrive as a stream; moderate accuracy suffices
AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adamas SGDone or two vectorsno simple guarantee in generalbadly scaled coordinates, sparse gradients, neural networks

Four rules of practice follow from the chapter. (1) Standardize the inputs before anything else (Section 7.4): it is the cheapest way to gain two or more orders of magnitude. (2) Regularization helps the optimization as well as the statistics: it adds λ\lambdaλ to the smallest curvature (Section 7.2.2). (3) For a smooth convex problem of moderate size, use a library solver (L-BFGS or Newton), which chooses its own step by line search; for large nnn, use SGD with mini-batches, a decaying step size tuned on a logarithmic grid, and monitor the training objective. (4) An iterative solver that stops at a fixed number of epochs is a regularized estimator: treat the number of iterations as a hyperparameter, to be chosen on validation data (Chapter 5), together with the other ones.

7.11 Summary¶

  • Gradient and steepest descent. The gradients of the least-squares, logistic and softmax losses all have the form (features) ×\times× (residual) and are checked by finite differences (relative error 10-8 to 10-10). The negative gradient is the steepest descent direction (Cauchy–Schwarz); gradient descent is wk+1=wk−η∇f(wk)\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k)wk+1​=wk​−η∇f(wk​).

  • Curvature. LLL-smoothness (∇2f⪯LI\nabla^2 f \preceq L\mathbf{I}∇2f⪯LI) and μ\muμ-strong convexity (∇2f⪰μI\nabla^2 f \succeq \mu\mathbf{I}∇2f⪰μI) define the condition number κ=L/μ\kappa = L/\muκ=L/μ. For least squares the eigenvalues of the Hessian are σj2/n+λ\sigma_j^2/n + \lambdaσj2​/n+λ, the singular values of Chapter 6. On Diabetes, κ=7.4⋅104\kappa = 7.4 \cdot 10^4κ=7.4⋅104 in raw units, 418 standardized, 37 with λ=0.1\lambda = 0.1λ=0.1 and 4.9 with λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1.

  • GD on a quadratic (Theorem 7.3). The error along the jjj-th eigenvector is multiplied by (1−ηλj)(1 - \eta\lambda_j)(1−ηλj​) per step: convergence iff η<2/L\eta < 2/Lη<2/L, best step 2/(L+μ)2/(L + \mu)2/(L+μ) with rate (κ−1)/(κ+1)(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)(κ−1)/(κ+1), at most κln⁡(1/ε)\kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon)κln(1/ε) iterations for η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L. On Diabetes: 5,6775{,}6775,677 iterations for η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L (predicted at most 5,7665{,}7665,766), 2,8562{,}8562,856 for the best step (2,8862{,}8862,886), divergence for 2.1/L2.1/L2.1/L.

  • Convex and strongly convex functions. The descent lemma gives f(wk)−f∗≤∥w0−w∗∥2/(2ηk)f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast \le \lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2/(2\eta k)f(wk​)−f∗≤∥w0​−w∗∥2/(2ηk) (Theorem 7.4) and, with strong convexity, the contraction ρ=max⁡{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣}\rho = \max\{\lvert 1 - \eta\mu\rvert, \lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert\}ρ=max{∣1−ημ∣,∣1−ηL∣} (Theorem 7.5). For the logistic regression on Breast Cancer the global bound L=3.30L = 3.30L=3.30 is 14 times the curvature at the minimizer (0.23): 1/L1/L1/L needs 1,6311{,}6311,631 iterations, η=8\eta = 8η=8 needs 69, and the threshold of stability is 2/Lloc=8.72/L_{\text{loc}} = 8.72/Lloc​=8.7 (above it the iteration ends in a cycle). The O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) bound holds and is loose by orders of magnitude.

  • Choosing the step. Backtracking with the Armijo condition terminates for every LLL-smooth function (Proposition 7.6): 57 steps and 169 function evaluations here. L-BFGS needs 19 iterations and Newton’s method 7, at a higher cost per step.

  • Conditioning. Rescaling the variables is preconditioning (Proposition 7.7): standardization is the Jacobi preconditioner and Newton’s method the ideal one. On Diabetes it reduces the iterations needed for a thousandfold reduction of the distance from 509,391509{,}391509,391 to 2,7992{,}7992,799; a ridge penalty of 0.1 reduces them to 176.

  • Momentum. The heavy ball has rate (κ−1)/(κ+1)(\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)(κ​−1)/(κ​+1) on quadratics (Theorem 7.8) and Nesterov’s method O(1/k2)O(1/k^2)O(1/k2) on every smooth convex function (Theorem 7.9, optimal). On Diabetes, 190 iterations against 2,8562{,}8562,856 for the best gradient descent; on the logistic regression, 146 against 1,6311{,}6311,631. Momentum methods are not descent methods.

  • SGD. The mini-batch gradient is unbiased with variance σ2/B\sigma^2/Bσ2/B, and the variance does not vanish at the minimizer (0.27 per example on Breast Cancer, against 5.8 at the start). A constant step gives a noise floor of order Lησ2/(2μ)L\eta\sigma^2/(2\mu)Lησ2/(2μ) (Theorem 7.11): on Breast Cancer 8.3⋅10−28.3 \cdot 10^{-2}8.3⋅10−2, 8.6⋅10−38.6 \cdot 10^{-3}8.6⋅10−3, 5.3⋅10−45.3 \cdot 10^{-4}5.3⋅10−4 for η=0.3,0.1,0.03\eta = 0.3, 0.1, 0.03η=0.3,0.1,0.03. A decreasing step ηk=β/(γ+k)\eta_k = \beta/(\gamma + k)ηk​=β/(γ+k) converges as O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) (Theorem 7.12): 3.4⋅10−53.4 \cdot 10^{-5}3.4⋅10−5 after 300 epochs. Averaging the iterates lowered a floor sixfold but did not remove it. The floor is ordered like η/B\eta/Bη/B (linear scaling rule). On this small problem full-batch GD (69 epochs to 10-8) is far better than SGD.

  • SGD in practice. On Digits the best step grows with the batch size (0.1/L0.1/L0.1/L, 1/L1/L1/L, 10/L10/L10/L, 30/L30/L30/L for B=1,16,128,1347B = 1, 16, 128, 1347B=1,16,128,1347); after 30 epochs the suboptimality is 0.0149 for full-batch GD against 0.0018 to 0.0044 for SGD, with test accuracies 0.956 against 0.969 to 0.971 (exact minimizer: 0.973).

  • Early stopping is implicit ridge. GD from zero multiplies the least-squares coefficient along the jjj-th eigenvector by 1−(1−ηhj)k1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^k1−(1−ηhj​)k, ridge by hj/(hj+λ)h_j/(h_j + \lambda)hj​/(hj​+λ), and with λ=1/(ηk)\lambda = 1/(\eta k)λ=1/(ηk) the first is between one and two times the second (Proposition 7.13; both bounds attained). On Diabetes the test MSE falls from 2848 to 2814 at k=7k = 7k=7; in raw units the path is monotone and never beats least squares: early stopping regularizes in the geometry of the parametrization.

  • Implicit bias. On separable data GD on the unpenalized logistic loss diverges in norm like ln⁡k\ln klnk and its direction converges, at rate O(1/ln⁡k)O(1/\ln k)O(1/lnk), to the maximum-margin direction (Theorem 7.14). On Iris the margin is at 96%96\%96% of the maximum after 103 steps and at 99%99\%99% after 104, the norm grows by 3.3 per decade at the end (theory: 3.57) and the angle is not monotone. On Breast Cancer (31 parameters) the direction converges far more slowly (angle 9∘9^\circ9∘ after 106 steps) and the early-stopped iterates classify better than the limit (Exercise 7.10).

  • Adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam) build a diagonal preconditioner from the gradient history. On raw Diabetes, GD still has a suboptimality of 86 after 3,000 iterations while Adam reaches machine precision; they are less sensitive to the scale of the inputs, not a substitute for standardizing them, and their constant-step behavior has overshoots and instabilities.

  • Non-convex functions. Saddle points repel gradient descent except from a measure-zero set: escape takes ln⁡(1/∣x0∣)/ln⁡(1+η)\ln(1/\lvert x_0\rvert)/\ln(1 + \eta)ln(1/∣x0​∣)/ln(1+η) plus a constant (≈28\approx 28≈28) iterations. With several minima the result depends on the initialization (four basins of about 25%25\%25% each for Himmelblau’s function).

Data sources¶

  • Diabetes: B. Efron, T. Hastie, I. Johnstone and R. Tibshirani, “Least Angle Regression”, Annals of Statistics 32(2), 407–499 (2004). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. The target is recoded so that malignant =1= 1=1.

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). The test portion of the data set, 1,797 images of 8×88 \times 88×8 pixels, is bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Iris: R. A. Fisher, “The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems”, Annals of Eugenics 7(2), 179–188 (1936). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Constructed functions and data (always flagged in the text): the quadratic 12(w12+10w22)\frac12(w_1^2 + 10w_2^2)21​(w12​+10w22​) of Worked example 7.1, the one-parameter logistic problem of Worked example 7.2, the three-point line fit of Worked example 7.3, and the two classical test functions of Section 7.9 (the double well and the Himmelblau function, D. M. Himmelblau, Applied Nonlinear Programming, McGraw-Hill, 1972). All the other experiments of the chapter use the real data sets above, and the exact minima f∗f^\astf∗ that they refer to were computed with Newton’s method or L-BFGS.

7.12 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 7.1 ★ — Gradient descent by hand. Let f(w)=w12+4w22f(\mathbf{w}) = w_1^2 + 4w_2^2f(w)=w12​+4w22​ and w0=(4,1)\mathbf{w}_0 = (4, 1)w0​=(4,1). (a) Compute the Hessian, LLL, μ\muμ, κ\kappaκ and the minimizer. (b) Run three steps of gradient descent with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L and write the general iterate. (c) What is the best constant step size, what is the rate, and what are the first three iterates with that step? (d) For which values of η\etaη does the iteration converge? Describe what happens for η=1/4\eta = 1/4η=1/4.

Exercise 7.10 ★★★ — Implicit bias on Breast Cancer. The Breast Cancer training set is linearly separable (Section 6.4.4). (a) Compute the hard-margin direction in the augmented space (standardized features and a constant column) with LinearSVC(C=1e6, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, dual=True, max_iter=5_000_000, tol=1e-10). (b) Run gradient descent on the unpenalized logistic loss with η=1/L\eta = 1/Lη=1/L for 106 iterations and, at k=10,102,…,106k = 10, 10^2, \dots, 10^6k=10,102,…,106, report ∥wk∥\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert∥wk​∥, the angle to the hard-margin direction, the ratio of the geometric margin to the maximum one, and the test accuracy. (c) Compare the test accuracy of the early-stopped iterates with that of the hard-margin classifier and comment: is the implicit bias of the limit the best thing to have?

Hint. The margin ratio is min⁡iyiwk⊤x~i/∥wk∥\min_i y_i\mathbf{w}_k^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i/\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVertmini​yi​wk⊤​x~i​/∥wk​∥ divided by 1/∥w^∥1/\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert1/∥w^∥, and is negative while the iterate does not yet separate the training set. The loop of 106 iterations is the slowest part of the exercise. The test set has only 143 patients: do not over-interpret small differences.

What comes next¶

We now have the machinery to compute the models of the book, and a precise understanding of what the computation does: its speed is governed by the conditioning of the problem, its noise by the batch size and the step, and stopping early is a form of regularization. Chapter 8 studies the support vector machine, obtained by replacing the logistic loss log⁡(1+e−m)\log(1 + e^{-m})log(1+e−m) by the hinge loss max⁡(0,1−m)\max(0, 1 - m)max(0,1−m). The hinge loss is not differentiable at m=1m = 1m=1, so Theorem 7.3 and its relatives do not apply directly: the next chapter will need subgradients or the dual problem, and will show that the solution depends only on the examples near the boundary, those that Section 7.7.3 called support vectors, for which the margin bound of Section 3.8.4 is the natural guarantee. Chapter 9 exploits the dual form of ridge regression (Proposition 6.12) to obtain kernels. Chapter 10 replaces the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty by the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty, which sets coefficients exactly to zero and performs feature selection, and which is again non-differentiable, so that plain gradient descent will not be enough. Chapter 11 returns to nonlinear models with decision trees and ensembles. In Part IV, Chapters 14 and 15 build neural networks and backpropagation, which is nothing but the computation of the gradient of Section 7.2.1 for a composition of functions; the optimizers of this chapter, SGD with momentum and Adam above all, are then used on non-convex losses, with the learning-rate recipes of Section 7.7.1.
